scenarios.title: Choose your main scenario
scenarios.subtitle: From 'I use it everywhere a little' to 'I apply it systematically'
scenarios.whatItIs:
A designer, a marketer and a PM have different AI stacks. The designer mostly uses Figma MCP + artifacts, the marketer — Projects with brand voice, the PM — [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] with a [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] per project. A scenario is a recipe for your role, not generic 'AI for everyone'.

A combo of 'task type + specific tool set'. Not 'I use Claude for everything', but 'I have a recurring audit → Project + Skill + [[node:mcp|MCP]]'. Narrow focus = mastery.
scenarios.approach: Don't try to cover all scenarios at once. One scenario brought to mastery pays off 10× more than 5 'I use it a little'. Start with a pilot on one task. Measure before/after. If it works — expand.

outcomes.0: Listed your 5 recurring tasks and identified the type of each
outcomes.1: Chose ONE main scenario — the most frequent
outcomes.2: Picked a stack for it: Project + Skill + (Code / MCP / API)
outcomes.3: Ran a pilot on a real task with measurement

s1.title: List your 5 recurring tasks
s1.why: Without a task list you can't choose a scenario meaningfully. This is the foundation.

instructions.0: Open your planner / tickets / calendar for the last month.
instructions.1: Write down 5 tasks that take the MOST time.
instructions.2: For each: type (analysis / code / design / content / research).

s1.example:
1. Regular audit of your materials — analysis
2. Preparing standard tasks for the team — content
3. Analyzing work results — analysis
4. Reviewing external information — research
5. Preparing reports / presentations — content
s1.validate: A list of 5 tasks with types. It's clear which type dominates.
s1.tip: The dominant type is your main scenario. Focus there.

s2.title: Choose the main scenario and tool stack
s2.why: Spreading Claude across everything — you get expert-level nowhere. Focus produces ROI.

instructions.0: Take the dominant task type from the list.
instructions.1: Pick a stack for it: Project + Skills + (Code / claude.ai).
instructions.2: Write it down: 'My main scenario — [type]. Tools — [list]'.

s2.example:
Main scenario: ANALYSIS (regular audit of your materials + results analysis).
Stack:
- Project for this process (with [[node:instructions|custom instructions]], knowledge base, cases)
- Skill for the audit routine (your own)
- MCP server to the relevant external system (if applicable)
Pen & paper: a list of risks and checks.
s2.validate: Main scenario + tool stack clearly formulated.
s2.tip: Don't try to cover all types. Better 'top' in one scenario per quarter than 'ok' in all five.

s3.title: Run a pilot on one real task
s3.why: A scenario 'on paper' is useless. Only a pilot will show whether it works.

instructions.0: Take ONE task from your backlog — the most typical in the chosen scenario.
instructions.1: Run it FULLY through Claude (using the chosen stack).
instructions.2: Measure time and quality. Compare with how you would have done it manually.

s3.validate: Task completed; you have a concrete measurement: time before/after, quality before/after.
s3.tip: If the pilot fails, don't abandon the tool. Ask: 'prompt?', 'stack?', 'context?'. 9 out of 10 problems are there.

s4.title: Document the workflow in a checklist
s4.why: Without a checklist the scenario falls apart in 2 weeks. The checklist = insurance against degradation.

instructions.0: Write down 5–7 steps of your tuned workflow.
instructions.1: Save in Notion / team README / any wiki.
instructions.2: Run every new task through the checklist.

s4.example:
# Workflow: <your recurring task>

1. Open the Project for this process in Claude
2. Load input data (URL / document / screenshot) into the chat
3. Activate the Skill for this routine
4. Get a report from the template (top-N problems + priority)
5. Transfer to your task tracker as linked tickets
6. After each cycle (week / sprint) — a mini-review of results
s4.validate: Checklist saved; you use it for every such task.
s4.tip: After 5–10 runs — revisit the checklist. Something always needs tweaking.

s5.title: Scale to the team
s5.why: One person with a scenario — fine. A team — leverage. This is where Claude truly changes how work gets done.

instructions.0: Share the workflow at a standup or in the work chat.
instructions.1: Find one colleague willing to try it.
instructions.2: After 2 weeks — compare notes. Expand the workflow.

s5.validate: At least one colleague is working with your scenario.
s5.tip: If the scenario works for YOU — it's a hypothesis. Two people — a pattern. Five — a team standard.

s6.title: Run a quarterly review and decide whether to expand
s6.why: A scenario is not an endpoint but a cycle. Once a quarter you need to tally the real payoff and consciously decide: deepen the current scenario or take on a second one. Without this ritual your focus quietly drifts back to 'I use it everywhere a little'.

instructions.0: Gather the quarter's measurements: total time saved, quality, how often the scenario is used.
instructions.1: Answer one question: is the main scenario brought to mastery (consistently paying off) — or not yet?
instructions.2: If YES — pick a SECOND scenario and repeat the cycle from 'List your 5 recurring tasks'. If NO — keep tuning the current stack and checklist for another quarter.

s6.example:
Quarterly review of the ANALYSIS scenario:
- Runs: 18
- Saved: ~4 h/week → ~50 h for the quarter
- Quality: reports more consistent, fewer missed problems
Decision: scenario pays off and is stable → take a second scenario — CONTENT (preparing reports / presentations) and run the cycle again.
s6.validate: You have a payoff figure for the quarter and a written decision: deepen the current scenario or launch a second one.
s6.tip: Expand only after stability. A second scenario on top of an untuned first one = the very spreading-thin we set out to escape.

scenarios.trigger: Generic AI posts don't help — you need a stack tailored to your role (PM / marketing / design).
scenarios.savings: ~3-5 hours/week on tasks specific to your function

claude-for-business.title: Claude for Business
claude-for-business.subtitle: Practical AI adoption for your team and workflows
claude-for-business.whatItIs: A practical course for business owners, managers, and team leads who want to integrate Claude into real work — not as an experiment, but as a reliable part of how their team operates. Covers identifying the right tasks, writing shared instructions, protecting sensitive data, measuring ROI, and scaling from one early adopter to a whole team.
claude-for-business.approach: This course works best if you take it with a specific business context in mind: your team, your recurring tasks, your constraints. Each step produces a concrete output — by the end you'll have a first draft of team instructions, a pilot task chosen, and a measurement plan. Theory is kept minimal; application is the point.
outcomes: Identified which business tasks deliver the most value when assisted by Claude
Written a shared team instruction set ([[node:b-system|system prompt]]) for your main use case
Applied a data privacy framework for what your team can and cannot input
Designed a 2-week pilot with before/after measurement criteria
Created a plan for expanding Claude use across your team

applyIn.title: Management and leadership
applyIn.description: Turn recurring decisions, reports, and reviews into templated AI-assisted workflows. Get drafts, summaries, and analysis in minutes rather than hours.

applyIn.title: Client-facing work
applyIn.description: Draft proposals, briefs, follow-up emails, and meeting summaries faster. Keep consistent tone and structure across team members.

applyIn.title: Internal operations
applyIn.description: Automate routine documents: HR templates, onboarding guides, policy summaries, process documentation. Reduce admin overhead without hiring.

pitfalls: Introducing Claude to the whole team at once without a pilot — adoption fails when people don't have concrete, successful examples first.
Skipping the instructions step — without shared context, each team member gets inconsistent results and concludes 'Claude doesn't work for us'.
Measuring the wrong metric — 'hours saved' sounds good but is hard to track; 'quality of first draft' and 'rounds of revision reduced' are more honest.

exercises.question: List 5 recurring tasks your team does weekly. For each, rate: (1) how time-consuming it is, (2) how much the quality varies between team members. Tasks that score high on both are your best candidates for AI assistance.
exercises.hint: Look for tasks where you've said 'we need a template for this' or 'why does everyone do this differently'.

exercises.question: Write a 5-sentence system prompt for your team's most common use case. Include: who Claude is acting as, what the goal is, what format to use, what to avoid, and who the audience is.
exercises.hint: Don't try to make it perfect. A 5-sentence prompt tested on 10 real tasks is worth more than a 50-sentence prompt that was never tested.

cb-1.title: Identify your highest-value AI tasks
cb-1.why: Most businesses start with 'let's try AI' and fail because they don't pick the right tasks first. A structured selection process ensures your pilot has the best chance of success.
instructions: The best business tasks for Claude share three properties: they recur frequently, they have a clear definition of 'good output', and they currently show quality variation between team members.

High-value categories: drafting documents (proposals, briefs, reports, emails), summarizing content (meeting notes, research, feedback), analyzing data or text (customer feedback themes, competitive positioning), creating templates and checklists.

Lower-value or risky categories: tasks requiring real-time data, decisions with significant financial or legal consequences (without human review), tasks where personal relationship or nuance is the whole point.

Your selection method: list 5 recurring tasks. Score each 1–3 on: frequency (how often), time cost (how long it takes), quality variance (how differently team members do it). Highest total score = your pilot task.
Important: pick ONE task for your pilot. Trying to fix everything at once is why most AI adoption initiatives stall.
cb-1.validate: You have identified one specific recurring task as your pilot — not 'communication' but 'first draft of client proposals' or 'weekly status report'.
cb-1.tip: The task you pick for your pilot will set the tone for your whole team's AI perception. Pick something where success is visible and measurable.

cb-2.title: Write shared team instructions
cb-2.why: The biggest reason AI doesn't 'work' for a business team is inconsistent instructions. When each person prompts differently, results vary. Shared instructions create shared quality.
instructions: Team instructions (a shared system prompt) tell Claude the context that never changes: who you are, what your business does, your tone and voice, and what 'good' looks like for your outputs.

Structure for a business system prompt:
  • Role: 'You are a business assistant for [Company], a [description]'
  • Audience: 'Our clients/colleagues are [description]'
  • Tone: 'Write in [formal/conversational/technical] style'
  • Format defaults: 'Use bullet points for lists, keep summaries under 200 words'
  • Constraints: 'Never mention competitor names, always include a next step'

Where to store shared instructions: in Claude, create a Project and add the instructions there. Everyone on the team uses the same Project. When instructions change, update once — it applies for everyone.
Start simple: 5–8 sentences is enough for a first version. You'll iterate based on what you observe in real use. Resist the urge to write an exhaustive prompt before testing.
Test your instructions: have 3 team members run the same task with the shared prompt. Compare outputs. Adjust what was inconsistent.
cb-2.prompt:
Template to adapt:

You are a professional assistant for [Company Name], a [brief company description]. Our clients are [client description].

Communication style: [formal/friendly/technical]. Default format: [bullet points/prose/structured sections]. Keep responses [concise/detailed] unless asked otherwise.

Always: [list 2-3 things to always do].
Never: [list 2-3 things to never do].
cb-2.validate: You have a draft team instruction set in a Claude Project that at least one other team member has tested.
cb-2.tip: Instructions are a living document. Schedule a 15-minute monthly review: what worked, what produced wrong outputs, what's missing.

cb-3.title: Data privacy: what your team can and cannot input
cb-3.why: Businesses handle sensitive data. The consequences of leaking client information, financial data, or personal data through an AI tool are real. A clear policy prevents both the risk and the uncertainty that makes people avoid the tool entirely.
instructions: Default rule for [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] (consumer product): treat it like a professional email to an unknown third party. Don't input what you wouldn't put in that email.

What's generally safe: anonymized descriptions of situations ('a client in the retail sector'), general business questions, document structures and frameworks, drafts that don't contain real names/numbers/identifiers.

What requires caution: actual client names and details (replace with 'Client A'), specific financial figures (use ranges or anonymize), employee personal data, legally privileged information, trade secrets or unreleased product plans.

Enterprise option: Anthropic offers enterprise agreements that include data privacy guarantees (no training on your data, security controls). If your business handles particularly sensitive data — consider this before rolling out to the full team.
Practical policy: create a one-page 'AI Input Policy' for your team. Three sections: OK to input, Input with caution (how), Never input. Make it specific to your industry and business context.
cb-3.validate: You have a draft AI input policy that you could share with your team today.
cb-3.tip: The goal of the policy is not to restrict AI use — it's to give your team confidence. 'Here's exactly what's safe' is more empowering than a vague 'be careful'.

cb-4.title: Design your 2-week pilot
cb-4.why: A pilot that isn't designed is just experimentation with no conclusion. A 2-week structured pilot gives you real data to decide whether to expand, adjust, or stop.
instructions: Define your pilot task: one specific, recurring task, used by 2–5 team members, over 2 weeks.
Baseline measurement: before starting, record how long the task currently takes and a quality score (1–5) for typical output. This is your control group.
Success criteria: decide now what 'good enough' looks like. Suggested: time reduced by ≥ 25%, quality maintained at same score or higher, team members report it's less frustrating.
During the pilot: everyone uses the shared instructions (the Project you created). Log: time taken, quality score, any notable failures or surprises.
End of pilot review: compare logged data to baseline. Decide: expand to more tasks, refine instructions, or stop. Either outcome is valuable — you've learned something real.
Common pilot failures to avoid: people forget to log, the task changes mid-pilot, 'good enough' wasn't defined upfront, instructions weren't finalized before starting.
cb-4.validate: You have a pilot plan: specific task, team members involved, start/end date, baseline recorded, success criteria defined.
cb-4.tip: Two weeks is long enough to hit the learning curve and short enough to maintain focus. Don't extend — run a second pilot instead.

cb-5.title: Measure ROI honestly
cb-5.why: AI ROI is often overstated in pilots and understated in long-term use. Honest measurement helps you make real decisions — including when to stop using Claude for something.
instructions: Time metrics: track actual time, not estimated. 'I think it saves me 2 hours' is usually wrong. Log the before and after for 10 real instances.

Quality metrics: count rounds of revision. If you spend less time revising, that's measurable value. If you spend more time fixing Claude's output than you would have writing it — that's a signal to stop.
Hidden costs: include time to write good prompts, time to review output, and time to train team members. ROI is net, not gross.

Strategic value: some tasks save no time but unlock new capability — analysis you wouldn't have done, insights from data you couldn't synthesize manually. Value these too, even if they're harder to quantify.

Decision framework: if time savings ≥ 25% OR quality improvement is noticeable OR a previously-impossible task is now possible — the task is worth continuing. Otherwise: stop, adjust, or move to a different task.
cb-5.validate: You have a simple spreadsheet or table tracking time and quality for your pilot task over 2 weeks.
cb-5.tip: Share your ROI data with your team. Real numbers from real work are far more persuasive than any vendor case study.

cb-6.title: Scale from 1 to your whole team
cb-6.why: A successful pilot means nothing if it stays with one person. Scaling requires a different set of actions than starting.
instructions: From pilot to standard: update your team instructions based on what you learned. Write a one-page 'How we use Claude' guide specific to the task you piloted.

Onboarding new users: don't just give people access and say 'try it'. Run a 30-minute session: show 3 real examples from your pilot, let them try the task themselves with the shared instructions, answer questions.
Identify your internal champion: the person who got the most value from the pilot. They should demonstrate use cases to colleagues — peer adoption is far more effective than management mandate.
Expand gradually: add one new use case every 4–6 weeks. Each new use case gets the same treatment: shared instructions, pilot, measurement, then standard practice.
Review quarterly: revisit all your Claude use cases. Are they still delivering value? Have new Claude capabilities made different approaches possible? Has your team's needs changed?
cb-6.validate: You have a 3-step onboarding plan for the next team member who will start using Claude for your piloted task.
cb-6.tip: The most common failure at this stage: moving too fast. One solid use case that 80% of your team uses reliably is worth more than 10 use cases that everyone tried once and forgot.

claude-for-business.trigger: The team uses Claude ad hoc — time to make it a reliable part of the process.

Learned to generate explanations at different levels of complexity

applyIn.title: School education
applyIn.description: Lesson plans, age-appropriate explanations, homework, test preparation.

applyIn.title: Higher education
applyIn.description: Lecture materials, practical case studies, grading rubrics, essay feedback.

applyIn.title: Corporate training
applyIn.description: Workshops, onboarding materials, knowledge-check quizzes.

pitfalls: Asking Claude to 'write a lesson' without context about your class and subject — you'll get a template, not material for specific students.
Delegating all student work assessment to Claude — the teacher's pedagogical judgment is irreplaceable.
Not telling students about AI use — transparency is critical for trust.

exercises.question: Choose a topic from your subject. Ask Claude to explain it in three ways: for a beginner, intermediate, and advanced level. Evaluate: which explanation would you use and what would you change?

ce-1.title: Why does an educator need Claude?
ce-1.why: Teachers spend up to 40% of their working time preparing materials. Claude takes on the draft work, leaving space for real interaction with students.
instructions: Claude plays three roles in education: draft generator (lesson plan, task, quiz), explainer (same topic at three difficulty levels in 30 seconds), feedback assistant (helps structure comments on student work).
What Claude does NOT do: it doesn't grade students for you, doesn't know your students personally, doesn't replace live classroom discussion.
Rule: use Claude to accelerate — not to replace pedagogical judgment.
ce-1.tip: Start with whichever task takes the most preparation time this week — a lesson plan, a set of tasks, feedback. That gives an immediate result.
ce-1.validate: Write down three tasks this week that take the most preparation time. These are your first candidates for Claude.

ce-2.title: Lesson preparation and materials
ce-2.why: Lesson plans, presentations, handouts — Claude creates all of these far faster. The key is giving the right context: subject, class, goal, constraints.
instructions: Use the request formula: Subject + Class/level + Topic + Lesson goal + Format + Constraints (duration, equipment, class specifics).

Example for a lesson plan: 'Subject: mathematics, grade 7. Topic: linear equations. Goal: student can solve a one-variable equation. Duration: 45 minutes. Three stages: explanation, practice, check. Add 5 problems easy to hard.'
Example for a differentiated task: 'Create a task on the topic ecosystem in three difficulty variants: basic (grade 6), standard (grade 8), advanced (grade 10). Each variant: 5 questions.'
Always add 'adapt for a real class, I will edit' — this tells Claude the result isn't final.
ce-2.tip: Save successful prompts in a Project as [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] — then Claude will know your subject and format from the first word.
ce-2.validate: Take a real lesson from next week. Describe it using the formula and ask Claude to create a plan. Note what's useful and what needs changing.

ce-3.title: Explaining complex topics
ce-3.why: Claude can explain one concept at any complexity level. This speeds up preparation for different groups without rewriting from scratch.
instructions: Use three prompts for one topic: 'Explain [topic] for an 8-year-old child', 'Explain [topic] for a 14-year-old without technical terms', 'Explain [topic] for a first-year university student with examples'.
Example — photosynthesis at three levels: age 8 — leaves cook food from sunlight and water; age 14 — chemical process without formulas; university student — light and dark phases in chloroplasts.
Extra prompts: 'Create an analogy to explain [concept]', 'What are common student misconceptions about [X]?', 'Create a comprehension check question for this topic'.
ce-3.tip: Always verify Claude's factual accuracy — especially for exact sciences, dates and region-specific details.
ce-3.validate: Choose a topic that's hard to explain at different levels. Ask Claude for three explanations. Use the best fragments in your next lesson.

ce-4.title: Tasks and tests
ce-4.why: Claude creates tests, case studies, rubrics and project briefs quickly and in the right format. Your role: set the parameters and edit the result.
instructions: For multiple choice: '10 questions with 4 options, topic X, level Y, add an answer key'.
For open-ended questions: '5 essay questions on topic X for grade 9'.
For a grading rubric: 'Create a rubric for a history essay (grade 9), criteria: argumentation, sources, structure, language. Scale 1–4, describe each level'.
For tiered tasks: '3 difficulty variants: easy, medium, hard — same topic'.
Save templates in a Project — create once, use all year.
ce-4.tip: Always ask for the answer key straight away — saves marking time.
ce-4.validate: Create a 10-question quiz on your next lesson's topic. Evaluate the quality and correct 2–3 questions that aren't accurate for your subject.

ce-5.title: Feedback and assessment
ce-5.why: Claude helps structure and phrase feedback — quickly and constructively. The teacher makes the final decision and adds personal context.
instructions: Claude handles well: structuring comments (what's good → what to improve → how to improve), rephrasing criticism into constructive language, generating typical comments for bulk marking.
Example prompt: 'I am an English teacher. A student wrote this essay: [text]. Criteria: structure, argumentation, grammar. Write constructive feedback in 3–4 sentences for a grade 10 student.'
For batch feedback: 'Here are my general comments to the class: [notes]. Turn them into 5 typical feedback responses I can adapt for different students.'
ce-5.tip: Never let Claude assign a grade without your decision. Grading is a pedagogical judgment, not an algorithm.
ce-5.validate: Take 3 student assignments. Use Claude for a draft of feedback. Compare with what you'd have written — where did Claude help, where did it miss?

ce-6.title: AI ethics in education
ce-6.why: Using Claude in education requires transparency with students, understanding its limits and a clear classroom policy. Ethics is the foundation of trust.
instructions: Principle 1 — Transparency: tell students when materials were created with AI. This builds critical thinking: 'Claude suggested this, I checked and adapted it'.
Principle 2 — Authorship: AI is a teacher preparation tool. Student work should be the student's work. Define clearly where AI helps learning and where it replaces it.
Principle 3 — Fact-checking: Claude can be wrong about dates, details and region-specific data. Always verify — especially in exact sciences and history.
Classroom policy template: AI may be used for brainstorming and drafts; final work must reflect the student's own thinking; using AI = citing the source.
For older students — teach them to work with Claude: it's a 21st-century skill. Assignment: 'write an essay and show how you used AI as a tool'.
ce-6.tip: A classroom policy works better when you create it together with students — they will suggest fair rules themselves.
ce-6.validate: Formulate AI-use rules for your class. Discuss them with students — their reaction will show what you missed.

applyIn.title: Marketing and communications
applyIn.description: A content machine with a consistent brand voice: long-form articles, SEO content, email campaigns and posts for multiple channels — Claude adapts one piece of content to all formats.

applyIn.title: Sales and Customer Success
applyIn.description: Personalised outreach, negotiation prep, objection analysis, response templates — Claude helps scale quality without losing personalisation.

applyIn.title: HR and operations management
applyIn.description: From writing JDs to onboarding packages and policies: Claude cuts time spent on administrative documents and helps maintain a consistent tone and standards.

pitfalls: Using one universal prompt for all tasks in the role — every scenario requires its own context and format. Create a separate template for each repeating task.
Publishing Claude-generated content without checking for brand alignment and factual accuracy — especially critical for external communications in sales and marketing.
Ignoring data confidentiality when working with customer or candidate information — use anonymised descriptions and do not input personal data unnecessarily.

exercises.question: Choose the three most time-consuming tasks in your role. Write a prompt for each and test it on a real example. Which of the three gave the best result on the first attempt?
exercises.hint: Tasks with a clear template and standard output format work best with Claude on the first try. Tasks requiring nuance and context improve after a few iterations.

exercises.question: Find a colleague from a different function (Marketing → Sales, HR → Product) and show them your best prompt. Ask them to adapt it to their role. What changed? What stayed the same?
exercises.hint: Prompt structure is usually transferable. Role context and output format change. This will show you what is the essence of the prompt and what is the role-specific layer.

ruc-1.title: Marketing: a content machine with a consistent voice
ruc-1.why: Marketing produces more content than any other function — but every piece must sound the same. Claude solves both challenges simultaneously.
instructions: Brand voice in the [[node:b-system|system prompt]]: add a brand voice description to the [[node:p-instructions|Project instructions]] — 3–5 adjectives, examples of sentences that sound 'right' and examples that sound 'wrong'. Claude will apply this automatically.

Long-form and SEO: a prompt for an article = topic + target audience + the main question the reader has + keywords + desired length + structure (H2/H3). Ask Claude to write the outline first and approve it before generating the full text.
Email campaigns: use one message as the base — ask Claude to create 3–5 variations of different length and tone (formal / conversational / urgent). A/B testing will show what works best.

Channel adaptation: one piece of content → five formats. Prompt: 'Here is the long-form text: [TEXT]. Adapt it for: (1) LinkedIn post 150 words, (2) Twitter/X thread of 5 tweets, (3) email subject line + preview text, (4) short summary for a newsletter, (5) script for a 60-second video'.
Typical marketer mistake: asking Claude to 'write content' without audience context. Always specify: who the reader is, what they already know, and how they should feel after reading.
ruc-1.tip: Create one reference piece in the Project that perfectly reflects the brand voice. Use it as a reference: 'Write in the same style as this example: [reference]'.
ruc-1.validate: You have created at least one prompt for a specific marketing task and received a result that can be used as a draft without major edits.

ruc-2.title: Sales: from lead to deal
ruc-2.why: Sales requires personalisation at scale — every message must feel hand-crafted, but doing it manually for 50 leads is impossible.
instructions: Personalised outreach: prompt = company profile (industry, size, recent events) + contact profile (role, pain points of the role) + your product + goal of the message (first contact / follow-up / re-engagement). Result: a draft message that only needs to be checked and personalised in 2–3 places.

Objection analysis: create an 'Objection Analysis' skill. Input: the customer's objection as stated. Output: (1) the real concern behind the objection, (2) 2–3 ways to respond, (3) a question that helps understand the depth of the issue.

Negotiation prep: prompt = company name + known deal information + your position + meeting goal. Ask Claude for: likely questions the customer will ask, likely objections, key arguments for your position, red lines that must not be crossed.

After the meeting: 'Here are my notes from the meeting: [NOTES]. Write a follow-up email with: (1) a thank-you, (2) a brief summary of agreements, (3) next steps with deadlines, (4) an open question to keep the dialogue going'.
Important: always verify factual data about the company and customer that Claude includes in messages — hallucinations in sales are especially dangerous.
ruc-2.tip: The best use of Claude in sales is not replacing personalisation but accelerating it. A draft in 30 seconds, personalisation in 2 minutes — instead of writing from scratch in 15 minutes.
ruc-2.validate: You have a template prompt for outreach that you have tested on 3 real leads and received drafts requiring minimal editing.

ruc-3.title: HR: from JD to onboarding
ruc-3.why: HR creates a large volume of repeating documents — and often spends time on them that could be spent working with people.
instructions: Job Descriptions: prompt = role title + key responsibilities (5–7 items) + must-have requirements + nice-to-have + team context + company format. Ask Claude to write a JD that: (1) sounds attractive to the target audience, (2) uses inclusive language, (3) avoids excessive requirements that exclude good candidates.

Structured interviews: 'I am hiring for [ROLE]. Here are 3 key competencies: [LIST]. For each competency create 2 behavioural questions (STAR format) and scoring criteria: excellent / good / insufficient'.

Welcome package for new employees: use a template prompt with variables — employee name, role, team, start date, manager. Claude generates a personalised welcome letter and first-week checklist in 2 minutes.

Policies and guidelines: 'Here is our existing [TOPIC] policy written 3 years ago: [TEXT]. Update it to current standards, make the language clearer, keep the substance. Mark where you made significant changes'.
Confidentiality: never input real candidate or employee names into Claude without their consent. Use initials or role descriptions instead of personal data.
ruc-3.tip: Create a library of template prompts for each HR document type in the Claude Project. One setup session saves several hours every week.
ruc-3.validate: You have written a JD or interview questions with Claude and compared the result to a previous version written manually. Which took less time and was the quality comparable?

ruc-4.title: Product: from Discovery to Spec
ruc-4.why: A Product Manager spends up to 40% of their time writing documents — PRDs, user stories, roadmap justifications. Claude does not replace product thinking but dramatically accelerates turning it into documents.
instructions: User Stories: 'Here are raw notes from user interviews: [NOTES]. Extract 5–7 user stories in the format: As a [role], I want to [action] so that [outcome]. For each add acceptance criteria and a priority (High/Medium/Low) with justification'.

Interview synthesis: 'Here are transcripts from 5 user interviews: [TRANSCRIPTS]. Extract: (1) recurring pain points (with mention frequency), (2) unexpected insights, (3) contradictions across interviews, (4) open questions requiring further research'.

PRD first draft: create a 'First PRD Draft' skill. Input: problem + target audience + proposed solution + constraints. Output: a PRD structure with completed sections and explicit placeholders where data that Claude does not have is needed.

Roadmap justification: 'I am proposing to prioritise [FEATURE] next quarter. Here is the context: [DATA]. Help write a justification for stakeholders including: business case, alternatives we considered, risks and how we mitigate them, success metrics'.
Important: PRD and roadmap contain strategic decisions that you make, not Claude. Use Claude for structure and wording — not for making product decisions.
ruc-4.tip: The best PRD workflow: first describe the problem to Claude in your own words in 5 sentences. Ask it to ask clarifying questions. Answer them. Only then ask for the document draft.
ruc-4.validate: You have used Claude to synthesise real data (interviews or notes) and received structured output that became the basis for a product decision or document.

ruc-5.title: Customer Success: scale without losing quality
ruc-5.why: A CS specialist handles many customers simultaneously — response quality inevitably drops under load. Claude helps maintain a high level at greater volume.
instructions: Response templates with personalisation: create a library of templates for the top 10 request types. Each template is a prompt with variables: customer name, product, issue summary, account context. Claude generates a personalised response based on the template in seconds.

Escalation: 'Here is the correspondence thread with the customer: [HISTORY]. The customer is expressing [DISSATISFACTION LEVEL]. Write: (1) a brief summary of the situation for the manager, (2) the proposed solution with justification, (3) a draft response to the customer'.

Health Score Analysis: 'Here is product usage data for the customer over the last 90 days: [DATA]. What patterns indicate churn risk? Which indicate expansion potential? Suggest 3 specific action items for the CS manager'.

QBR preparation: 'Here is the account data for the quarter: [DATA]. Help prepare a QBR: (1) key achievements that matter specifically to this customer, (2) ROI visualisation, (3) recommendations for the next quarter, (4) open questions for discussion'.

Boundary of application: Claude does not see the relationship history with the customer that you have built. Always provide factual details (figures, agreements, names) explicitly — never assume Claude 'knows' the customer.
ruc-5.tip: The fastest win for CS: create a template for the most frequent request type. The first hour of setup pays off in the first week.
ruc-5.validate: You have a ready response template for at least one request type that you have tested on real cases and it requires minimal editing before sending.

ruc-6.title: Build your role playbook
ruc-6.why: Scattered prompts living in notes do not produce a systemic effect. A playbook turns them into a standard — your personal one or your team's.
instructions: Role playbook structure: (1) Top 5 role tasks with prompts, (2) Recommended Project structure (instructions + knowledge base), (3) Common mistakes to avoid, (4) How to assess output quality, (5) What to never delegate to Claude.
Choose your top 5 scenarios: list five tasks you do every week. For each write a prompt, add an example input and expected output. This is the core of the playbook.
Document anti-patterns: record 2–3 cases where Claude gave a bad result and why. This is the most valuable part of the playbook for colleagues — they learn from your mistakes, not their own.
Format for sharing: a Claude Project with instructions is ideal for storing a playbook. Share access with the team — or export as a Notion/Confluence page with prompts ready to copy.
Living document: add a 'last updated' date and a 15-minute retrospective once a month. Claude and its capabilities change — the playbook must change with them.
ruc-6.tip: The best playbook is minimal but used. Five well-described scenarios beat twenty formal ones. Start small and add as you use it in real work.
ruc-6.validate: You have a role playbook with at least three documented scenarios that you are ready to send to a colleague today. Check: could they use it without your explanations?

role-use-cases.trigger: Basics are solid — time to assemble a working stack for a specific role (Marketing / Sales / HR / Product / CS).
inputs: Your function and top 5 weekly tasks
outputs: Role playbook: 5 tasks × ready prompt + Project
Onboarding plan for peers in the same role

uc-ai-reporting-launch.title: Launch AI Reporting
uc-ai-reporting-launch.subtitle: A ready scenario: from manual reports to a working weekly report workflow in 2 weeks
uc-ai-reporting-launch.whatItIs: A step-by-step route to move a regular report (weekly/monthly) onto Claude: from a manual draft to a repeatable workflow used by the team. Built on a chain of 105 Atlas nodes — [[node:prompting|Prompting]], [[node:projects|Projects]], [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]], [[node:ops-reporting-automation|Reporting Automation]], [[node:sc-data|working with data]].
uc-ai-reporting-launch.approach: Quality first, automation later. AI writes a draft → a human edits → measure quality on 5-10 real reports. Only after stable results do you add triggers and scheduling. A two-week cycle: Day 1-3 setup, Day 4-7 iterations, Day 8-14 roll-out.
outcomes: A working weekly report workflow in 2 weeks
Time-to-report cut from 4 hours to 30 minutes
Report consistency up ~90% (single format)
The team can use the workflow and trusts it (NPS survey)
The report format is fixed and reused instead of rebuilt every time

applyIn.title: Operations / business analytics
applyIn.description: Weekly summaries of sales, funnel, and metrics from CRM and analytics with CSV export.

applyIn.title: Management reporting
applyIn.description: Regular reports for leadership: project status, KPIs, concise digests from many sources.

applyIn.title: Team / department updates
applyIn.description: Recurring team summaries where the format is stable and data refreshes each period.

pitfalls: Wanting full automation in the first week — get draft quality right first, then add triggers
Starting without available data: if there is no CRM/analytics export, the workflow stalls
Rewriting the format from scratch each time instead of fixing it in [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
Rolling out to the team before 5-10 successful manual iterations — no trust, no feedback
Not measuring results: without time-to-report and NPS metrics you cannot prove value

exercises.question: Which of your reports fits the first launch and why exactly that one?
exercises.hint: Look for a regular report taking ≥3 hours per week, with available data and a stable format.

exercises.question: What fields and structure should the final report have so they can be described in CLAUDE.md?
exercises.hint: Take 1-2 past reports and list the sections, metrics, and tone — that is your future format.

exercises.question: How will you know the workflow is ready to roll out to the team?
exercises.hint: Use the criterion: 5-10 real reports in a row with acceptable draft quality.

s1.title: When the scenario is needed and what you get
s1.why: Without a clear trigger and expected result, the team drowns in "start reading everything". This step confirms the scenario applies at all and locks in a measurable outcome.
instructions: Check the trigger: there is a regular report (weekly/monthly) taking ≥3 hours per week
Check data: it is available via CRM/analytics export (CSV, etc.)
Check buy-in: the team agrees to try a new workflow
Lock target metrics: time-to-report 4h→30min, consistency +90%, NPS survey
State the outcome in one phrase: "a working weekly report workflow in 2 weeks"
s1.validate: You have one concrete candidate report, access to its data, and recorded target metrics.
s1.tip: If the trigger or the data is missing, do not launch yet — it saves you two weeks.

s2.title: Preparation: data, access, context
s2.why: Report quality is capped by input quality. This step prepares the data and a shared workspace so iterations run without stopping to ask "where do the numbers come from".
instructions: Gather data sources and confirm export works (see [[node:sc-data|working with CSV data]])
Create a shared "Weekly Reports" workspace for the team via [[node:projects|Projects]]
If the report needs CRM context, learn how to feed it to Claude ([[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]])
Take 1-2 past reports as a reference for format and tone
Agree on who owns the workflow and who edits drafts
s2.validate: Data exports cleanly, the workspace exists, reference reports are at hand.
s2.tip: Start with a single data source — do not try to connect everything at once.

s3.title: First draft: prompt and format
s3.why: This is the heart of the scenario: teach Claude to write the report in the right format. Manually at first, to see real quality and find what to improve.
instructions: Write a system prompt for the report (see [[node:prompting|Prompting]] and [[node:b-system|system prompt]])
Describe the report format — sections, metrics, tone — in the workspace [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
Feed real data for one period and get a first draft
Compare the draft against the reference report and note the gaps
Record what the AI does well and what you have to fix by hand
s3.validate: You have a first coherent draft, and the format lives in CLAUDE.md and is reused.
s3.tip: Do not chase perfection on the first try — the goal is a working starting point.

s4.title: Iterate on real reports
s4.why: One draft proves nothing. Stable quality only shows on a series of real reports — this is where the workflow matures into something repeatable.
instructions: Run 5-10 real reports as: AI draft → human edits → log the edits
After each iteration refine the prompt and format in [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
Shape the stages into a repeatable process following [[node:ops-reporting-automation|Reporting Automation]]
Measure editing time — it should drop from iteration to iteration
Collect frequent edits into a checklist so the prompt covers them upfront
s4.validate: 5-10 reports in a row produce an acceptable draft, and manual editing steadily decreases.
s4.tip: If editing is still heavy after 10 iterations, the issue is the data or the format, not Claude.

s5.title: Quality check and risks
s5.why: Before going to the team you must confirm the report is accurate and reproducible — one wrong number would undermine trust in the whole workflow.
instructions: Reconcile the draft's numbers against the source data — check for factual errors
Test stability: the same data yields a comparable result
Record the measured time-to-report and compare with the 30-minute target
Define which parts require mandatory human review
Describe the risk zones (sources with dirty data, sensitive metrics)
s5.validate: Quality is confirmed by the check, metrics are met, mandatory-review spots are known.
s5.tip: Add full automation only after this step — never before.

s6.title: Roll-out and scaling
s6.why: Value appears when the whole team uses the workflow, not just one author. The final step is the roll-out, gathering feedback, and cementing the practice.
instructions: Run the team roll-out: show the workflow and the shared workspace [[node:projects|Projects]]
Collect feedback and run an NPS survey (likelihood to recommend, 0-10)
Add automation — triggers and scheduling — following [[node:ops-reporting-automation|Reporting Automation]]
Assign an owner who maintains the prompt and format in [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
Readiness checklist: format in CLAUDE.md, 5-10 successful iterations, metrics met, team trained, owner assigned
s6.validate: The team uses the workflow, NPS is collected, automation is added, the checklist is closed.
s6.tip: Once one report is dialed in, the same path repeats easily for the next — the format already exists.

uc-ai-process-automation.title: Automate a Recurring Process
uc-ai-process-automation.subtitle: From an operations process your team does by hand every week to a production workflow on Skills and Hooks with quality checks
uc-ai-process-automation.whatItIs: A structured path to automating one specific recurring process via AI: from choosing a good candidate to a production-ready workflow with [[node:skills|Skills]] and automatic triggers. Not "we tried Claude and liked it", but a systematic approach with metrics and quality gates.
uc-ai-process-automation.approach: First pick and stabilize a process that runs at least 5 times a week with clear inputs/outputs. Then document it as-is and identify the steps AI can realistically take over. Build the automation core — a reusable Skill plus external integrations if needed — and add triggers. Always embed quality gates with human review, test on historical data, and only then roll out to production with monitoring and a scaling plan.
outcomes: An automated workflow for a specific process, ready for daily use in 2-3 weeks
70-90% time savings on the routine steps of the process
Error rate below 5% thanks to quality gates and human review
A reusable Skill you can apply to similar processes
Clear before/after metrics to prove the value to your team and leadership

applyIn.title: Incoming request handling
applyIn.description: Classifying, enriching, and routing tickets or requests that arrive by the dozen each day in a single template.

applyIn.title: Producing regular documents
applyIn.description: Weekly reports, summaries, client emails — where the format is stable and manual variability gets in the way.

applyIn.title: Routine data operations
applyIn.description: Moving, reconciling, normalizing data between systems via [[node:mcp|MCP]] integrations when the steps repeat and are well described.

pitfalls: Automating a process that isn't stabilized yet — the workflow will break with every change
Skipping quality gates: without human review, automation produces trash at scale
Picking a process that is too complex or too rare — no savings, and maintenance eats your time
Testing only on "convenient" examples and ignoring edge cases from historical data
Rolling out to production without monitoring — errors pile up unnoticed and team trust drops

exercises.question: Find one process in your team that runs ≥5 times a week with clear inputs and outputs. Describe its steps and mark which ones AI could take over.
exercises.hint: A good candidate: stable format, clear result, measurable time. If the process still changes every week, stabilize it first.

exercises.question: For the chosen process, design 3 quality gates — points where the result is checked before moving on. Where is a human strictly required?
exercises.hint: Think about irreversible actions: sending to a client, changing data, financial operations. Cover those with human review first.

exercises.question: Define a before/after success metric for your automation: how much time is spent now and what target error rate is acceptable.
exercises.hint: A practical benchmark: 70-90% time savings and an error rate below 5%. Capture the baseline BEFORE launch, or you have nothing to prove value with.

s1.title: When you need it and the target outcome
s1.why: Without the right candidate, automation either won't pay off or will keep breaking. This step decides whether to start at all.
instructions: Check candidate criteria: the process runs ≥5 times a week with clear inputs and outputs
Confirm that result variability in manual execution is a real problem for the team
Verify technical feasibility: do you have access to the needed triggers and integrations
State the expected outcome in metrics: 70-90% time savings, error rate <5%
Look at [[node:ops-process-automation|Process Automation]] as the target structure with quality gates
s1.validate: You have one specific process and a written goal in measurable before/after metrics.
s1.tip: If torn between two processes, take the one that repeats more often and changes less. Frequency × stability = payoff.

s2.title: Preparation: document the process as-is
s2.why: You can't automate what isn't described. The as-is document shows which steps AI can take over and which must stay with a human.
instructions: Write out the process step by step as it runs today (Week 1)
For each step note: inputs, action, result, who/what is responsible
Mark the AI-replaceable steps — where Claude can produce a stable result from clear rules
Collect a set of historical examples for future tests (real cases, including edge cases)
Make sure the process is stable — if it still changes, lock it down first
s2.validate: You have a step-by-step map of the process, marked AI steps, and a set of historical examples for tests.
s2.tip: Edge and "awkward" cases from history are worth more than a dozen typical ones — that's exactly where the workflow breaks in production.

s3.title: Execution: the automation core — a Skill
s3.why: A reusable Skill is the instruction Claude applies the same way every time. It turns a one-off prompt into a systematic process.
instructions: Build the workflow core as a Skill via [[node:s-create|Creating a Skill]] — describe the goal, steps, and output format
Lean on [[node:skills|Skills]] so the Skill is self-contained and reusable
Work out the core workflow prompt following [[node:prompting|Prompting]] rules
Run the Skill on the historical examples from step 2 and compare with the real results (Week 2)
Tune the prompt to a stable output on both typical and edge cases
s3.validate: The Skill produces the expected result on historical examples, including some of the edge cases.
s3.tip: Don't try to cover everything with one giant prompt. A clear Skill with a defined output format is more reliable than a wall of instructions.

s4.title: Execution: integrations and triggers
s4.why: The Skill handles "what to do", while integrations and triggers handle "where the data comes from" and "when to run". Without them, automation stays a manual button.
instructions: If external systems are needed, connect them via [[node:mcp|MCP]] (data sources, team tools)
Set up automatic triggers via [[node:cc-hooks|Claude Code Hooks]] — by event, schedule, or incoming request
Wire the chain: trigger → data via MCP → Skill → result
Run the full path end-to-end on test data, not just the Skill itself
Record which steps stay manual and why (part of the quality gates)
s4.validate: The full path from trigger to result runs on test data with no manual intervention on the automatic steps.
s4.tip: Start with one trigger and minimal integrations. Extra connections complicate debugging and widen the surface for errors.

s5.title: Quality checks and risks
s5.why: Quality gates are the main defense against "automated trash". Without checks, errors pile up at scale and destroy team trust.
instructions: Embed quality gates: points where the result is checked before moving on
For irreversible actions (sending to a client, changing data, money) keep a mandatory human review
Measure the actual error rate on historical data and compare with the <5% target
Test edge cases separately — they reveal the weak spots of the workflow
Describe a rollback plan: what to do if automation produces a wrong result
s5.validate: The error rate is within target, risky steps have human review, and there is a rollback plan.
s5.tip: A quality gate isn't a slowdown — it's insurance: better to route 100% of results through review the first week than fix your reputation later.

s6.title: Rollout, scaling, and checklist
s6.why: A production launch without monitoring and a scaling plan turns a working prototype into an unmanaged risk. This step locks in the value.
instructions: Roll the workflow out to production with monitoring of results and error rate (Week 3)
Capture the after metrics and compare with the baseline from step 1 — prove the savings to the team
Decide whether to expand the approach: stage transition 1→2 (first automation) or 2→3 (scaling)
Find similar processes that reuse the same Skill and add them to the queue
Run the checklist: candidate fits / process documented / Skill stable / triggers and MCP work / quality gates in place / monitoring on
s6.validate: The workflow runs in production, the after metrics confirm the value, and the checklist is fully passed.
s6.tip: Write up the case: process, metrics, gotchas. It's both proof of value and a template for the next automation from the [[node:use-cases|Use Cases]].

uc-ai-decision-support.title: AI Support for Operational Decisions
uc-ai-decision-support.subtitle: From "let us discuss in Slack" to a structured decision process with AI analysis in 3-4 weeks
uc-ai-decision-support.whatItIs: This course shows how to bring AI into your team's operational decisions — not as "the decider", but as a tool for structuring and pattern matching. You will build a working decision process where AI prepares trade-off analysis and surfaces past cases, while the human makes the call and owns accountability.
uc-ai-decision-support.approach: Operations teams make 5-10 decisions a week under load: lots of reactive, little learning. This approach adds discipline without bureaucracy — a lightweight template, AI analysis via [[node:prompting|structured prompting]], and a decision log in [[node:projects|Projects]]. Start with a pilot of 3-5 decisions, then refine and roll out with a retrospective.
outcomes: A working decision process with AI support in 3-4 weeks
Reactive decisions drop by 50-70%
A learning loop is established: retrospective with AI pattern matching over decision history
A "Decision Log" with outcome tracking for future retrospectives
The team clearly understands AI's boundaries: where it adds value, and where accountability stays with the human

applyIn.title: Hiring and recruiting
applyIn.description: Hire vs no-hire decisions with trade-off analysis: AI structures the arguments for and against, the human weighs context and decides.

applyIn.title: Vendor and tool selection
applyIn.description: Vendor selection by matching criteria and pricing: AI assembles data into one structure and surfaces similar past choices from the log.

applyIn.title: Process changes
applyIn.description: Process change decisions: AI pattern-matches against past changes ("we decided this a year ago"), reducing repeat mistakes.

pitfalls: Using AI as "the decider". AI is good at structuring and pattern matching, but context and accountability belong to the human.
Ignoring documentation. Tracking outcomes matters more than the AI output itself: no log means no learning loop.
Overloading the process with bureaucracy. A heavy template kills adoption — keep it light.
Putting every decision into the process at once. Start with major decisions that need trade-off; leave the small stuff as is.
Trusting AI output without checking the data. Weak inputs lead to confident-sounding but wrong analysis.

exercises.question: List 5 decisions your team made last month. Which required trade-off analysis and would fit AI support, and which would not?
exercises.hint: Candidates: hires, vendors, process changes. Non-candidates: obvious operational actions with no alternatives.

exercises.question: Take one past decision the team later regretted. What data and arguments would AI have helped structure beforehand?
exercises.hint: Think about what was known at the time but never pulled into one picture.

exercises.question: State a boundary: which decision would you NOT trust AI to even structure? Why?
exercises.hint: Look for decisions tied to hidden context, people, or ethics — that is where AI is blind.

s1.title: Define when the scenario is needed and the target outcome
s1.why: Without a clear scope, AI support turns into bureaucracy for every decision. First decide which decisions to include at all.
instructions: Collect the types of decisions your team made over a month (hires, vendors, processes).
Mark those that require trade-off analysis — these are candidates for AI support.
Define the expected outcome: a working process in 3-4 weeks, reactive decisions down 50-70%.
Fix the goal: structuring and a learning loop, not handing decisions to AI.
s1.validate: You have a short list (3-5 types) of decisions where AI support adds value.
s1.tip: If a decision is obvious and has no alternatives, it does not belong in this process.

s2.title: Prepare the data and context for analysis
s2.why: AI analysis quality equals input data quality. Weak input leads to a confident-sounding but wrong conclusion.
instructions: For each decision type, define what data is needed (numbers, criteria, constraints).
Learn to feed data to AI via [[node:prompting|structured prompting]] — facts separate from the question.
Set up a "Decision Log" workspace in [[node:projects|Projects]] for history and context.
Collect 2-3 past decisions as a reference for future pattern matching.
s2.validate: For the pilot decision, you can quickly assemble a clean set of data and context.
s2.tip: Separate "facts" from "the question for AI" — it sharply improves structuring quality.

s3.title: Step 1: structure trade-off analysis with chain-of-thought
s3.why: The key to value is making AI reason step by step and lay out arguments for and against, rather than spitting out a ready answer.
instructions: Build a prompt template on [[node:prompting|prompting principles]]: context → data → task → output format.
Ask AI to expand its chain-of-thought: criteria, options, pros/cons of each.
Fix the output format: a trade-off table plus AI's explicit assumptions.
Run it on 1 simple pilot decision and assess how useful the structure is.
s3.validate: AI produces a readable trade-off breakdown with explicit assumptions, not a single "answer".
s3.tip: Always ask AI to name its assumptions — that reveals where it might be wrong.

s4.title: Step 2: add pattern matching over decision history
s4.why: The core operations pain is "we decided this a year ago and forgot". History in the log turns past decisions into a learning loop.
instructions: Give AI access to the "Decision Log" in [[node:projects|Projects]] as context.
Ask AI to find similar past decisions and their outcomes before a new conclusion.
For each new decision, record: context, options, choice, expected outcome.
After 1-2 cycles, verify AI actually surfaces relevant past cases.
s4.validate: On a new decision, AI references similar past cases from the log.
s4.tip: Record not just the choice but the expected outcome — otherwise the retrospective has no teeth.

s5.title: Quality and risk check: the human decides, not AI
s5.why: AI is good at structuring and pattern matching, but context and accountability belong to the human. Without this barrier the process is dangerous.
instructions: Set the rule: AI output is an input for discussion, not a decision.
Check AI's assumptions and the data its analysis was built on.
Flag decisions where hidden context/ethics/people make AI blind — there it only structures.
Pin down who is accountable for each decision (a human, not the model).
s5.validate: The team understands: the final decision and accountability always rest with the human.
s5.tip: If AI sounds too confident, treat it as a signal to re-check the input data.

s6.title: Rollout and the rollout checklist
s6.why: The pilot proves value; rollout with a retrospective turns it into a durable team process.
instructions: Week 1: pilot on 3-5 simple decisions.
Week 2-3: refine the template and verify quality on real cases.
Week 4: roll out to all major decisions + the first retrospective with AI pattern matching.
Checklist: lightweight template, log in [[node:projects|Projects]], the "human decides" rule, outcome tracking.
s6.validate: The process works across all major decisions, reactive decisions have dropped, the first retrospective is done.
s6.tip: Keep the template light: heavy bureaucracy kills adoption faster than poor AI output.

uc-ai-content-ops-launch.title: Launch AI Content Operations
uc-ai-content-ops-launch.subtitle: From generic AI texts to a content machine with brand voice in 2 weeks
uc-ai-content-ops-launch.whatItIs: A step-by-step scenario that turns scattered AI use across a team into a working content pipeline with a recognizable brand voice. Not "AI writes faster" but "AI writes the way we write" — systematically, with quality checks and rollout to the team.
uc-ai-content-ops-launch.approach: The core of the scenario is brand voice. First you capture the brand voice and templates (preparation), then you build the two key pipeline steps (brief→draft and review→edit), and only then scale to the team. Without voice work the pipeline just produces generic texts faster — so voice setup is ~30% of the effort and must not be skipped.
outcomes: You understand when the scenario fits and the concrete result it delivers (time-to-publish, consistency, volume)
A documented brand voice as a reusable doc and system prompt
A working pipeline: brief → draft → review → publish with clear roles at each step
A quality and tone check that separates "sounds like us" from "sounds like AI"
A rollout checklist the team uses to scale the process without losing quality

applyIn.title: Marketing team with inconsistent AI
applyIn.description: The team already uses AI ad-hoc but texts sound different. The scenario brings everyone to one voice and predictable quality.

applyIn.title: Blog and regular content >10 pieces/month
applyIn.description: Once volume grows, hand-editing every draft does not scale. A pipeline with voice cuts time-to-publish dramatically.

applyIn.title: Launching a new content stream
applyIn.description: A new product or section needs a voice from scratch. The scenario gives the frame: voice, templates, review — before chaos accumulates.

pitfalls: Building the pipeline without voice work — you get generic texts faster, but still generic
Treating brand voice as "a couple of adjectives" instead of concrete attributes with "do / don't" examples
Skipping the tone review — speed goes up but AI style leaks into published pieces
Rolling out to the whole team at once without test pieces and voice-prompt iteration
Not measuring results — without time-to-publish and consistency you cannot tell if it improved

exercises.question: Assemble a brand voice doc: 5 voice attributes, each with a "do / don't" pair using real phrases from your brand.
exercises.hint: Pull wording from your best published pieces, not from your head. Voice is what already works.

exercises.question: Run one piece through the full pipeline (brief→draft→review→publish) and time each step.
exercises.hint: The before measurement is your baseline. Without it you cannot prove time-to-publish dropped.

exercises.question: Give a colleague 3 texts: 2 of your published ones and 1 AI draft without voice. Can they tell which is which?
exercises.hint: If the AI text is easy to spot, the voice is still weak — add specifics to the system prompt.

s1.title: Decide when the scenario is needed and lock the target result
s1.why: The scenario pays off only under certain conditions. Launching a pipeline "just in case" without volume and without editor buy-in wastes time and yields no measurable effect.
instructions: Check the triggers: team already uses AI ad-hoc, quality is inconsistent, volume >10 pieces/month, editor/content lead buy-in exists.
Record baseline metrics: current time from draft to publish, share of pieces "on brand voice", monthly volume.
State the target result: e.g. time-to-publish 2 days→4h, brand consistency 60%→90%, volume +200%.
If even one trigger is missing (no volume or no buy-in) — postpone the scenario, otherwise the pipeline will not stick.
s1.validate: You have 3 baseline numbers and 3 target numbers — something to compare against in 2 weeks.
s1.tip: This scenario is the path from Foundation to Transformation. If basic prompting still wobbles, start with [[node:prompting|writing briefs]].

s2.title: Preparation: brand voice and templates
s2.why: Brand voice is the core of the whole scenario (about 30% of the effort). Without an explicitly described voice any pipeline produces generic texts, just faster.
instructions: Audit existing content: pick 5-10 best pieces and write down voice attributes (tone, vocabulary, sentence length, what the brand never says).
Capture the brand voice as a [[node:b-system|system prompt]] and mirror it with profile-level [[node:instructions|custom instructions]] for everyday chats.
Create a [[node:projects|"Blog" Project]] and put voice files, "do / don't" examples and brief templates into it.
For the team workspace add a [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] with voice rules if you work in Claude Code.
s2.validate: You have a voice doc + a Project with voice files; on a test phrase Claude answers in the right tone without long briefing.
s2.tip: A voice attribute without a "do / don't" example is useless. Claude learns from contrast, not from adjectives.

s3.title: Key step 1: brief → draft
s3.why: This is the pipeline input. Draft quality is 80% determined by brief quality — no editing will rescue a weak input.
instructions: Lock a brief template: topic, goal, audience, key points, format, length, what NOT to write.
Generate the draft inside the "Blog" Project so voice files are pulled in automatically.
Run 3-5 test pieces and iteratively fix the voice prompt where Claude drifts off tone.
Lock the final draft prompt as part of the Project — it is a reusable asset.
s3.validate: On a new brief the draft comes out on brand voice with minimal edits and no manual re-briefing.
s3.tip: If drafts vary in quality, the problem is in the brief, not in Claude. Standardize the input first.

s4.title: Key step 2: review → edit
s4.why: This is the pipeline output control. Without an explicit review step AI style leaks into published pieces and the whole speed gain is wasted.
instructions: Describe the review step as part of a sequential pipeline — see the [[node:sys-linear-chain|linear chain]] (brief → draft → review → publish).
Give Claude an editor role: check brand voice fit, facts, structure and return a list of edits, not a silent rewrite.
Introduce a tone checklist: "sounds like us?", no clichés or AI markers, banned phrasings respected.
Run 2-3 pieces through the draft→review pair and compare the result against the voice doc.
s4.validate: After the review step a piece passes the tone checklist and edits from a human editor are minimal.
s4.tip: Review ≠ re-generation. Ask for a list of edits with reasons — that shows you where the voice breaks systematically.

s5.title: Quality and tone check at scale
s5.why: One good article is luck. Before handing the pipeline to the team you must confirm quality and tone are stable across a series of pieces.
instructions: Build a set of 5 varied pieces (different topics/formats) and run the whole pipeline end to end.
Rate each against the tone checklist and compare with the baseline metrics from step 1.
Blind test: give a colleague a mix of published and AI pieces — if the AI ones are spotted, strengthen the voice prompt.
Record typical tone failures and add counterexamples to the Project and voice doc.
s5.validate: Across 5 different pieces consistency stays at the target level; the blind test does not reveal the AI texts.
s5.tip: Measure, do not "feel". Consistency 90% is a concrete share of pieces passing the checklist, not an impression.

s6.title: Rollout, scale and a team handoff checklist
s6.why: The scenario delivers value only when the team uses it, not a single person. The final step turns the work into a repeatable process.
instructions: Describe the finished process as [[node:mk-content-ops|content operations]] with roles and metrics; for separate deep voice tuning use [[node:mk-brand-voice|brand voice tuning]].
Share the Project, brief templates and voice doc with the whole team; assign a voice owner who keeps it updated.
Run the rollout: a short walkthrough + 1-2 joint runs so the team can repeat it without you.
Turn on measurement: track time-to-publish, consistency and volume weekly for the first 2 weeks.
Go through the handoff checklist: voice doc current, Project shared, pipeline steps documented, metrics tracked, owner assigned.
s6.validate: At least one colleague runs a piece through the whole pipeline on their own, and weekly metrics confirm the gains.
s6.tip: Assign a voice owner. Without one the voice doc goes stale within a month and the pipeline quietly slides back to generic.

uc-ai-support-tier1.title: Launch AI Tier-1 Support
uc-ai-support-tier1.subtitle: From "all by hand" to "AI closes 40% of tickets" in 4 weeks
uc-ai-support-tier1.whatItIs: A how-to course on rolling out AI first-line support (Tier-1 — simple, repetitive questions) step by step in a real team. This is not "buy a bot" but a structured path: knowledge base first, then AI, then quality control and human escalation. One of the highest-ROI AI projects in support.
uc-ai-support-tier1.approach: The order of steps is strict and deliberate: the knowledge base (KB) comes first, because AI answers only as well as the KB it retrieves from (RAG). First we prepare the ground, then assemble the AI scenario, then embed quality control and safe escalation, and only then roll out to live traffic via a pilot and metrics. See the pattern in [[node:ai-native-customer-support|AI-native customer support]] and [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]].
outcomes: A working AI Tier-1 with deflection (share of tickets closed by AI without a human) around 40%
Median response time on AI tickets drops from 4 hours to 2 minutes
CSAT (customer satisfaction score, 1-5) does not drop relative to baseline
Clear boundaries: what AI answers itself versus what it escalates to a human
A repeatable process for expanding from 1 ticket category to 3-5

applyIn.title: High volume of typical questions
applyIn.description: Tier-1 generates >100 tickets per week, and most are repeating questions with known answers in the knowledge base.

applyIn.title: Something to compare against
applyIn.description: A baseline CSAT and response time "before AI" exists, otherwise you cannot prove the rollout actually helped rather than hurt.

applyIn.title: Willing to invest 3-4 weeks
applyIn.description: There is buy-in from the CS lead and product team, and 3-4 weeks can be allocated to KB prep, setup and a pilot.

pitfalls: Launching AI Tier-1 without KB prep — KB ops are 50% of the work, and without them AI answers generic or wrong
Using an outdated or poorly structured KB — AI retrieves garbage and confidently returns a wrong answer
Skipping escalation setup — AI starts "choking" complex tickets instead of handing them to a human, and CSAT collapses
Rolling out to all categories at once instead of a single-category pilot — you cannot see where quality breaks
Not setting up quality control (random sample review) — answer degradation goes unnoticed until a wave of complaints

exercises.question: You have 250 Tier-1 tickets per week, but the knowledge base is two years old and articles were written by different people with no consistent structure. Where do you start — bot setup or the KB?
exercises.hint: Recall the order rule: AI answers only as well as the KB. What happens to retrieval if article structure is poor?

exercises.question: The pilot shows 40% deflection, but CSAT on AI tickets is 0.4 below baseline. What do you check first?
exercises.hint: Think about AI boundaries and escalation: maybe AI is taking on tickets it should have handed to a human.

exercises.question: Which single metric do you show the CS lead to prove the pilot's value in week one?
exercises.hint: The metric must reflect savings (deflection) yet not mask a quality drop — which is why it is always read alongside CSAT.

s1.title: Understand when the scenario fits and what success looks like
s1.why: Without a clear launch criterion and a measurable goal, the project becomes "let's try a bot" and quietly dies. First confirm you truly have a Tier-1 task and define what counts as success.
instructions: Check the volume threshold: Tier-1 generates more than 100 tickets per week — otherwise manual work is cheaper than automation
Record the baseline: current CSAT and median response time "before AI" — this is your reference point
State the goal in numbers: 40% deflection, response time 4h→2min, CSAT no lower than baseline
Get buy-in from the CS lead and the product team (product is needed for KB access)
s1.validate: You have a one-pager: ticket volume, baseline metrics, target numbers, and agreement from both teams.
s1.tip: If baseline metrics are missing — collect them for a week before starting. Without a reference point you cannot prove impact.

s2.title: Prepare the knowledge base and set AI boundaries
s2.why: This is 50% of all the work. AI retrieves answers from the KB (the RAG mechanism), so a bad KB means confidently wrong answers. Here we also decide which questions AI answers itself and which go to a human.
instructions: Audit existing KB articles: drop outdated ones, merge duplicates, bring them to a consistent structure
Re-chunk long articles into atomic pieces — so retrieval fetches the exact answer, not "a whole article about everything"
Using [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]], verify the KB is retrieval-ready: clear headings, facts not marketing
Define boundaries: a list of categories where AI answers itself, and stop-topics (billing, legal, complaints) that always go to a human
s2.validate: The KB is cleaned and structured, and there is an explicit "AI answers" / "human only" list.
s2.tip: Take 20 real recent tickets and check by hand whether the KB yields a correct answer. If it doesn't, AI won't either.

s3.title: Assemble the AI ticket-answering scenario
s3.why: The key step: the answering AI is born here. The system prompt sets tone, format and rules, and the connected KB provides the facts. Without a careful prompt, AI answers generic and off-brand.
instructions: Write the support bot system prompt: role, tone of voice, answer format, the rule "if you don't know — escalate, don't invent"
Create a dedicated workspace (Project) and connect the cleaned KB from step 2
Require a source citation from the KB in the prompt — so the answer is verifiable and does not hallucinate
Run 15-20 typical questions and refine the prompt until answers are accurate and on-brand
s3.validate: On typical questions AI answers correctly, in the right tone, with a KB citation, and on stop-topics it proposes escalation itself.
s3.tip: The rule "better to honestly say I don't know and escalate than to invent" matters more than a nice tone — it protects CSAT.

s4.title: Embed quality control and human escalation
s4.why: AI without safe human handoff is dangerous: it will "choke" complex tickets and drag satisfaction down. And without sampled review, answer degradation stays invisible until a wave of complaints.
instructions: Set up escalation routing: on which signals a ticket goes to a human (stop-topic, low confidence, explicit customer request)
Make handoff seamless: the human gets the ticket with full conversation context, not from scratch
Launch random sample review: a random selection of AI answers is checked by a human for correctness
Create a simple answer-scoring checklist: accuracy, tone, source citation, appropriateness of escalation
s4.validate: Any doubtful ticket goes to a human with context, and a portion of AI answers is regularly reviewed against the checklist.
s4.tip: At launch, set the escalation threshold aggressively: better to hand a human too much than to break trust with a wrong answer.

s5.title: Pilot on one category and measure metrics
s5.why: Rolling out to everything at once hides where quality breaks. A single-category pilot gives a clean signal: does the KB + AI + escalation chain work on real traffic?
instructions: Pick one high-volume, low-risk ticket category (for example, "how to reset a password")
Launch AI on that category and measure deflection and CSAT every day
Compare AI-ticket CSAT to baseline — a drop is a signal to fix the prompt or boundaries, not to scale
Collect failing cases from review and return to steps 2-3 to refine the KB and prompt
s5.validate: On the pilot category deflection climbs toward 40% while CSAT holds at baseline.
s5.tip: Don't scale until CSAT has stabilized: rising deflection alongside falling CSAT is a loss, not a success.

s6.title: Rollout, metrics and readiness checklist
s6.why: After a successful pilot you need to expand coverage without losing quality and lock in the process, so the rollout is repeatable rather than a one-time feat.
instructions: Expand AI to 3-5 categories one at a time, repeating the deflection and CSAT measurement each time
Lock in a dashboard with three metrics: deflection rate, median response time, CSAT vs baseline
Make quality review a regular ritual (for example, a weekly sample), not a one-off
Run the readiness checklist: KB current, boundaries set, escalation works, metrics on the dashboard, review on the calendar
s6.validate: AI steadily closes ~40% of Tier-1 across several categories, metrics are visible on a dashboard, and the process is documented and repeatable.
s6.tip: Assign a KB owner: an aging knowledge base is the main cause of slow AI-support degradation months later.

uc-ai-discovery-launch.title: Launch AI Discovery in Your Product
uc-ai-discovery-launch.subtitle: From manual research to an AI-powered discovery pipeline in 2 weeks
uc-ai-discovery-launch.whatItIs: A step-by-step scenario that turns scattered interviews and feedback into a working AI-discovery pipeline. You organize the research repository, set up RAG-based synthesis, and embed it into your product process with validation. This is an applied route from the [[node:use-cases|Use Cases]] set, built on the [[node:pd-discovery-research|Discovery Research]] practice.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.approach: We move by the principle "input first, then synthesis, then process".
