First we clean up the data (without structured input AI is useless), then we set up two key synthesis steps — theme extraction and conclusion framing — then we verify the conclusions on familiar interviews, and only then embed the pipeline into the team's regular work. Each step produces a verifiable result, not "setup for the sake of setup".
outcomes: The research repository is organized: all interviews and feedback in one place, accessible to AI
Working synthesis: from data to structured themes in ≤2 hours per topic instead of days of manual work
100% research coverage — AI reads the whole corpus, not just the 30% you reach manually
Conclusions are verified and backed by source links, trustworthy for decision-making
The pipeline is embedded in the product process and scales to new feedback flow without manual synthesis

applyIn.title: Product team with accumulated research
applyIn.description: ≥30 interviews or ≥100 feedback items left unprocessed — the scenario turns the archive into a source of insight.

applyIn.title: Slow discovery → ship cycle
applyIn.description: When data synthesis is the bottleneck and decisions stall, the pipeline cuts time-to-insight down to hours.

applyIn.title: Building an [[node:ai-native-product|AI-native product]]
applyIn.description: When the team makes AI part of the work itself rather than a one-off experiment, discovery becomes the first reproducible loop.

pitfalls: Running synthesis without structured input: if interviews are scattered across Notion, Google Docs and Slack, AI won't find them
Underestimating data prep — organizing the repository takes ~30% of the whole scenario and cannot be skipped
Trusting conclusions without verification: synthesis without source-checking produces plausible but wrong themes
Stopping at interviews and not extending the pipeline to ongoing feedback — then the system goes stale within a month
Setting up the pipeline solo and not training other PMs — the knowledge stays with one person and doesn't stick

exercises.question: Where do your interviews and feedback live right now, and why won't AI find them in their current state?
exercises.hint: List every storage location. If there's more than one and no single repository — that's your Day 1 work.

exercises.question: How will you know an AI conclusion is correct rather than a plausible fabrication?
exercises.hint: Think about source links: every theme should point to specific interview quotes.

exercises.question: What happens to the pipeline in a month if you set it up only on old interviews?
exercises.hint: Think about the flow of new feedback — whether a separate step for ongoing data is needed.

s1.title: Understand when the scenario is needed and lock in the outcome
s1.why: The scenario pays off only with real data volume and leadership support. Without that, you automate emptiness.
instructions: Check the entry threshold: ≥30 interviews or ≥100 feedback items without structured processing
Confirm the discovery → ship cycle is truly slow because of synthesis, not other causes
Get buy-in from the Head of Product — without it the pipeline won't stick in the process
Lock in target metrics: time-to-insight ≤2 hours per topic, 100% research coverage
s1.validate: You have a written scenario goal and the product leader's agreement.
s1.tip: If you have less data than the threshold, the scenario is premature — accumulate research first or the setup won't pay off.

s2.title: Prepare the input: gather research into a single repository
s2.why: Without structured input AI won't find the data — the main reason the scenario fails. Prep takes ~30% of the total time.
instructions: Gather all interviews and feedback from Notion, Google Docs, Slack into one place
Create a [[node:projects|Project]] "Discovery Workspace" and upload the research files there
Normalize the files: clear names, date, source
Set up the RAG foundation ([[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]]) so AI can search the whole corpus
s2.validate: All research materials sit in one repository and are searchable via AI.
s2.tip: Don't try to process the whole backlog at once — 5-10 interviews are enough for debugging.

s3.title: Key synthesis step #1: theme extraction
s3.why: Theme extraction is the foundation of discovery. The quality of themes determines how useful all later conclusions will be.
instructions: Frame a synthesis prompt for extracting recurring themes (based on [[node:prompting|Prompting]])
Run it on 5-10 test interviews from the repository
Require each theme to reference specific quotes from sources
Compare the result against what you know about those interviews manually
s3.validate: AI produces a structured list of themes with source links, and the themes are recognizable.
s3.tip: Ask for themes with frequency and examples, not "general conclusions" — they're easier to verify.

s4.title: Key synthesis step #2: connect context and frame conclusions
s4.why: Themes alone aren't conclusions. Context must be passed correctly between steps so synthesis doesn't lose the thread.
instructions: Set up context passing between synthesis steps ([[node:sys-context-passing|Context Passing]])
Turn themes into product conclusions: problem, frequency, who is affected
Embed PM validation gates — points where a human checks the conclusion before use
Assemble the whole process into a reproducible [[node:pd-discovery-research|Discovery Research]] workflow
s4.validate: Themes yield clear conclusions stating the problem and its scale, passing through PM review.
s4.tip: Context is easily lost on large corpora — pass only the condensed essence between steps, not raw text.

s5.title: Verify the reliability of conclusions
s5.why: AI produces plausible but sometimes false themes. Without verification the team will decide based on a fabrication.
instructions: Take 5-10 interviews you know well and check AI conclusions against reality
Confirm each theme is backed by references to specific quotes
Note discrepancies and refine the synthesis prompts based on validation feedback
Document the working prompt patterns that produce reliable results
s5.validate: Conclusions match your manual understanding of familiar interviews, discrepancies resolved.
s5.tip: If AI "invented" a theme with no quotes — that's a signal to refine the prompt, not to ignore the error.

s6.title: Embed into the process and extend to ongoing feedback
s6.why: One-off synthesis goes stale. The scenario's value is a regular pipeline embedded in the team's work.
instructions: Scale synthesis to the full research backlog
Extend the pipeline to ongoing feedback ([[node:pd-feedback-synthesis|Feedback Synthesis]]), not just interviews
Train other PMs to run the pipeline themselves
Lock in a checklist: repository updated → synthesis run → conclusions pass validation → decision
s6.validate: The pipeline runs on a regular data flow, several PMs use it, and a process checklist exists.
s6.tip: Assign an owner for maintaining the repository — without fresh data the pipeline quickly loses value.

uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.title: Enterprise AI Transformation Roadmap
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.subtitle: How to build a roadmap that moves a company from ad-hoc pilots to AI-native operations in 12 months
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.whatItIs: This is the highest-level scenario in the [[node:use-cases|Use Cases catalog]] — for CEOs, CIOs, and Heads of AI. The roadmap describes a company's full path from "doing AI pilots ad-hoc" to "AI-native company-wide operations": enterprise strategy → tactical department roll-outs → org-wide change with governance and ROI measurement. Horizon: 6-12 months of work.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.approach: A roadmap is built not as a feature list but as a sequence of phases. First you decide whether transformation is even needed and what the target outcome is, then you honestly assess organizational readiness. Next comes prioritization of initiatives (which directions and in what order), launching pilots with quick wins, establishing governance and risk management, and only then scaling across the whole company. Key principle: directions are launched sequentially (one per quarter), not all at once.
outcomes: A 12-month roadmap document broken down by quarters with clear gates between phases
A prioritized list of tactical directions with rationale for the launch order
A governance framework and risk register in place before scaling begins, not after an incident
A set of metrics and a target ROI agreed with the executive team before the first pilot
A scaling-readiness checklist: what must be complete before expanding to a new direction

applyIn.title: Board and executive team
applyIn.description: The roadmap becomes the single document where the board sees where money goes, the expected ROI, and which risks are under control.

applyIn.title: Center of Excellence (CoE)
applyIn.description: A team of 3-5 people uses the roadmap as an operational plan: what to launch this quarter, what to measure, what to carry into the next.

applyIn.title: Department heads
applyIn.description: Each direction owner sees when their department enters the transformation and which quick wins are expected from the first pilot.

pitfalls: Launching all 4 tactical directions in parallel in Q1 — a recipe for chaos and team burnout
Starting pilots without an enterprise strategy and governance — incidents will later halt the whole program
Choosing the first direction because it is "trendy" rather than by ROI and data readiness
Failing to fix metrics before launch — six months in, there is nothing to prove the effect to the board
Assuming Stage 4 (full AI-native maturity) is reachable in 12 months — realistically it is Stage 1→3, with Stage 4 another 12-18 months

exercises.question: Your company is launching an AI transformation. You have executive buy-in and an 18-month budget. Where do you start in Q1 — with strategy and the CoE, or straight into two pilots?
exercises.hint: Recall the phase logic: pilots without strategy and governance are vulnerable to the first incident. Q1 is the foundation (strategy, CoE, governance) plus selecting the first directions — not launching them all.

exercises.question: You need to pick the first tactical direction for a pilot. Tier-1 support gives fast ROI, while marketing gives strategic impact. How do you decide?
exercises.hint: In a roadmap you usually take the direction with the highest and fastest ROI first (often Support tier-1) to get a quick win that funds the next phases. Strategic directions go second.

exercises.question: Six months in, the board asks what the transformation delivered. What should you have prepared at the very start to answer with numbers?
exercises.hint: Metrics and target ROI are fixed BEFORE the first pilot. Without baseline measurements you cannot show the uplift — this is built into the governance/measurement phase, not added retroactively.

s1.title: Define when a roadmap is needed and what the target outcome is
s1.why: A roadmap makes sense only when the company commits to transformation strategically, not by running isolated pilots. Without a clear goal and executive buy-in, any plan falls apart midway.
instructions: Check the preconditions: is there executive buy-in and a resource commitment ($M+ budget) for 12-24 months
State the target outcome: e.g., "company at Stage 3 AI-native operations in 12 months"
Define top-level target metrics: number of tactical directions, documented ROI, share of AI-proficient team
Make it explicit that this is a Stage 1→3 path in 12 months, with Stage 4 in the next 12-18 months (managing board expectations)
s1.validate: You have a one-page description of the roadmap goal with a measurable target state and confirmed executive buy-in.
s1.tip: If there is no executive buy-in or a 12+ month budget, this is not a roadmap but a single pilot. Do not launch a transformation without a commitment from the top.

s2.title: Run an organizational readiness audit
s2.why: You cannot prioritize initiatives without knowing the starting point. The audit shows which stage the company is at and where the bottlenecks are — data, skills, infrastructure.
instructions: Assess the current maturity stage: ad-hoc pilots, isolated teams, or some existing systematization
Check data and infrastructure readiness for each potential direction
Assess the team's AI proficiency and where upskilling is needed (talent strategy)
Record the presence or absence of a CoE, governance, and change-management processes
s2.validate: You have a readiness map: current stage, strong and weak zones across data, skills, and processes.
s2.tip: Honesty beats optimism. An inflated readiness estimate leads to choosing directions that fail due to poor data.

s3.title: Prioritize tactical initiatives and set the launch order
s3.why: The main transformation mistake is launching everything at once. Prioritization by ROI and readiness sets a sequence where each previous direction teaches the organization the next.
instructions: Build a list of candidate directions from the [[node:ai-native-enterprise|AI-native enterprise]] (support, operations, product, marketing)
Score each on two axes: size and speed of ROI, data/team readiness
Assign the order: 1 direction in Q1, the 2nd in Q2, the 3rd in Q3, the 4th in Q4
Take the fastest-ROI direction first (often Support tier-1), and the most strategic one second (Product or Marketing)
s3.validate: You have an ordered list of 4 directions with a rationale for the order based on ROI and readiness.
s3.tip: Each previous direction is a lesson for the organization. Sequential rollout is not about caution but about accumulating competence.

s4.title: Launch pilots and lock in quick wins
s4.why: A quick win in the first pilot proves value, funds the next phases, and creates momentum for company-wide change management.
instructions: Alongside the foundation from the [[node:en-transformation-strategy|enterprise transformation strategy]], form the CoE team (3-5 people)
Launch tactical pilot #1 on the highest-ROI direction, limiting scope to a narrow scenario
Launch pilot #2 on a strategic direction, start the change program and the AI upskilling roll-out
Document quick wins in money/time and use them as the argument for the next phase
s4.validate: Two pilots are launched, and there is at least one documented quick win with numbers.
s4.tip: Narrow the pilot scope aggressively. A tight scenario with a clear metric delivers a win faster than "AI for the whole department".

s5.title: Establish management, risks, and governance
s5.why: Without governance and a risk register, the first incident (leak, hallucination, reputation) will halt the whole program. Management must run ahead of scaling, not chase it.
instructions: Implement a governance framework: who makes decisions, which AI usage policies are mandatory
Set up a formal risk register: privacy, security, output quality, regulation
Set up ROI measurement: a baseline before the pilot and regular measurement over the first 6 months
Task the CoE with spreading best practices org-wide so directions do not repeat each other's mistakes
s5.validate: A governance framework, risk register, and ROI measurement system with a recorded baseline are in operation.
s5.tip: Governance is not bureaucracy but insurance. One uncontrolled public incident can freeze the entire transformation budget.

s6.title: Plan scaling and pass the checklist
s6.why: Scaling means adding new directions and moving toward maturity. A readiness checklist ensures you expand on a healthy foundation rather than replicating chaos.
instructions: Add directions #3 and #4 sequentially, building on the learnings from previous quarters
Run a strategy refresh: rebuild the roadmap based on actual results
Prepare an annual board report: ROI, new capabilities, risk status
Pass the expansion-readiness checklist: is ROI documented, does governance work, is the team 80%+ trained, are there no open critical risks
s6.validate: All 4 directions are launched, there is an annual board report, and the readiness checklist for the next maturity phase is passed.
s6.tip: Do not expand to a new direction until the previous one has passed the checklist. Skipping the readiness gate is the main reason transformations stall at Stage 2.

uc-ai-rag-launch.title: Launch a RAG System
uc-ai-rag-launch.subtitle: From "AI doesn't know our documents" to a working pipeline with citations in 6 steps
uc-ai-rag-launch.whatItIs: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a pattern where the LLM retrieves relevant fragments from your knowledge base before answering, and responds strictly from them with [[node:cap-citations|citations]]. This course goes from deciding "do we need RAG" to a production pipeline: corpus prep, indexing, answer assembly, quality evaluation, and shipping to prod. It's the technical foundation of most AI projects in [[node:use-cases|use-cases]].
uc-ai-rag-launch.approach: We move from simple to reliable, but do NOT stop at Naive RAG. First we fix why RAG is needed and what we measure. Then we build the pipeline in layers: corpus → embeddings + vector DB → answer assembly with citations → evaluation → prod. At each step we check quality on real questions, not "by eye". The production minimum is chunking with overlap, hybrid search, and re-ranking — otherwise users will see "the AI says wrong things".
outcomes: You know when RAG is needed and when a plain prompt or fine-tuning is enough
A pipeline is built: corpus → embeddings → vector DB → retrieval → answer with citations
Every answer is backed by source links (citation rate 100%)
There is a measurable quality metric: retrieval relevance and hallucination level
The system ships to production via a checklist: latency, monitoring, corpus updates

applyIn.title: Support and internal knowledge base
applyIn.description: AI answers staff and customers from your policies and ticket history, not from the model's general knowledge — with a link to the exact document.

applyIn.title: Document work and compliance
applyIn.description: Finding answers across contracts, policies, regulations. Citations are critical: a reviewer must see where a fact comes from.

applyIn.title: Product docs and onboarding
applyIn.description: A user asks in natural language, RAG retrieves the exact docs fragment and answers from it instead of making them read the whole page.

pitfalls: Naive RAG in production: query → vector → top-K → LLM yields 50-60% accuracy. You need re-ranking, hybrid search, chunk overlap, metadata filtering
Bad chunking: chunks too large blur relevance, too small lose context. Ignoring overlap loses meaning at boundaries
No quality evaluation: shipping "by eye" without measuring retrieval relevance and hallucinations — the system breaks silently
Answers without citations: users can't verify a fact and don't trust the system; you lose RAG's key edge over a bare LLM
Forgetting corpus updates: the index goes stale, RAG answers from old documents and presents outdated facts as truth

exercises.question: For your scenario: RAG, fine-tuning, or just a prompt with context? Justify the choice.
exercises.hint: RAG — when knowledge changes often and citations are needed. Fine-tuning — when style/format changes, not facts. Prompt with context — when there are few documents and they fit the window.

exercises.question: Take 10 real user questions and for each define which corpus fragment MUST land in the answer. This is your retrieval evaluation gold set.
exercises.hint: Without a gold question-answer set you can't measure relevance. Start with 10-20 pairs — enough for a first quality check.

exercises.question: Design chunking for one type of your documents: chunk size, overlap, which metadata to attach.
exercises.hint: Base it on document structure (paragraphs/sections), not a blind fixed character count. Metadata (source, date, section) is needed for filtering and citations.

s1.title: Decide: do you need RAG and what do you measure
s1.why: RAG is the most common production pattern, but not universal. Without a clear "why" and a metric, you'll build a pipeline you can't evaluate or improve.
instructions: State the problem: where exactly the LLM "doesn't know our facts" (documents, KB, history)
Check alternatives: is a prompt with context enough, or is fine-tuning needed — see [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG basics]]
Fix target metrics: answer accuracy, citation rate, latency per query
Describe the baseline: current accuracy without RAG (usually ~30%)
Define the application direction (Operations/Marketing/Support/Product/Enterprise)
s1.validate: You have a one-sentence "why RAG" and 3 measurable metrics with target values.
s1.tip: If knowledge barely changes and fits the context, you may not need RAG — a prompt is enough.

s2.title: Prepare the corpus: document chunking
s2.why: Retrieval quality is capped by chunk quality. Bad chunking is a ceiling on the whole system's accuracy that no re-ranking can fix.
instructions: Collect a pilot set of documents of one type (not the whole corpus at once)
Pick a chunking strategy: by semantic blocks (paragraphs/sections), not blindly by characters
Set chunk overlap so meaning isn't lost at fragment boundaries
Attach metadata to each chunk: source, date, section — for filtering and citations
Clean noise: navigation, footers, duplicates
s2.validate: Pilot documents are split into chunks with overlap and metadata; manually checking 5-10 chunks shows coherent meaning.
s2.tip: Start with pilot data, not the whole corpus — you'll spot chunking issues faster and redo them cheaper.

s3.title: Indexing: embeddings + vector DB
s3.why: Embeddings turn chunks into vectors for semantic similarity search. The vector DB stores them and enables fast retrieval — the heart of the pipeline.
instructions: Choose an embedding model fit for your documents' language and domain
Choose a vector DB: pgvector / Pinecone / Weaviate for your scale and stack
Run pilot chunks through embeddings and load vectors with metadata into the DB
Set up hybrid search (keyword + semantic), not vector search alone
Check retrieval on the gold questions from the exercise: do the right chunks land in top-K
s3.validate: For gold questions, the right chunk consistently lands in the top-K retrieval results.
s3.tip: Hybrid search covers pure vectors' weakness on exact terms, codes, and names — it almost always lifts relevance.

s4.title: Assemble the answer with citations
s4.why: Retrieval found fragments — but the answer must rely strictly on them and link to the source. Without [[node:cap-citations|citations]], users can't verify facts and don't trust the system.
instructions: Assemble the pipeline per [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]: at least Advanced RAG, not Naive
Add re-ranking: re-sort top-K by relevance before passing to the LLM
Pass the retrieved context to the LLM with instruction to answer ONLY from it
Enable [[node:cap-citations|citations]]: every fact linked to a source from metadata
Add "I don't know" behavior when retrieval has no answer — instead of inventing one
s4.validate: On test questions the answer relies on retrieved fragments, includes citations, and honestly says "no data" when there is none.
s4.tip: Re-ranking is the cheapest quality lever: even a simple re-ranker noticeably lifts the relevance of top results.

s5.title: Evaluate quality: relevance and hallucinations
s5.why: Shipping "by eye" means the system breaks silently. You need numbers: how well retrieval fetches the right thing and how well answers stick to facts.
instructions: Run the gold question-answer set from the exercise through the pipeline
Measure retrieval relevance: does the right chunk land in top-K
Measure hallucination level: are there facts in answers without source backing
Check citation rate: does every answer link to a real fragment
Find weak spots and return to chunking (s2) or retrieval (s3) surgically
s5.validate: There is a metrics table over gold questions; accuracy approaches target (85%+), hallucinations are rare.
s5.tip: Low quality is more often fixed at chunking and retrieval than by swapping the LLM — first check the right chunk is even found.

s6.title: Production: ship to prod and checklist
s6.why: A pipeline in a notebook and one in prod are different. Production needs latency, monitoring, and regular corpus updates, or the system degrades.
instructions: Check latency per query (<500ms target) and optimize bottlenecks
Set up corpus updates: how new documents enter the index
Enable monitoring: query logs, retrieval quality, share of "no data"
Add user feedback on irrelevant answers
Run the checklist: s1 metrics met, citations work, corpus is updatable
s6.validate: The system in prod answers within the latency target, the corpus updates, and s1 metrics are confirmed on live traffic.
s6.tip: Build corpus updates in from the start — a stale index quietly serves old facts as current.

uc-ai-pilot-to-production.title: Moving an AI Pilot to Production
uc-ai-pilot-to-production.subtitle: From "the pilot works" to reliable AI in prod: readiness criteria, reliability, evals, monitoring, security, and rollout with a rollback plan
uc-ai-pilot-to-production.whatItIs: A structured transition from a successful AI pilot to a production system with quality gates, monitoring, and governance. A cross-layer scenario: systems quality + enterprise risk management + foundational safety. It closes the most common stall point where AI projects die: "the pilot worked, but scale-up got stuck."
uc-ai-pilot-to-production.approach: We don't rebuild the pilot from scratch — we add the missing production layers: formalize readiness criteria, add error handling and reliability, set up objective quality evaluation (evals), turn on monitoring and cost control, pass governance/access review, and roll out gradually with a rollback plan. Each step produces a verifiable artifact — without it, the step isn't done.
outcomes: A production-ready AI system in 4-6 weeks instead of endless pilot "polishing"
0 high-severity incidents in the first 90 days thanks to reliability and a rollback plan
Objective quality evaluation (evals) instead of "we think it works"
Transparent monitoring and cost: you see degradation and spend before they become a problem
Documented governance compliance: data classification, access, and risks captured and approved

applyIn.title: Customer-facing AI service
applyIn.description: A chatbot or assistant piloted with a subset of users is rolled out to the full audience with an SLA, response-quality monitoring, and a rollback plan.

applyIn.title: Internal process automation
applyIn.description: AI document or request processing that proved out on one team scales across the company with governance data review and cost control.

applyIn.title: AI in a product touching real money/brand
applyIn.description: Content generation, recommendations, or decisions affecting revenue or reputation move to prod with evals, access audit, and a gradual rollout.

pitfalls: Skipping the governance review under "but the pilot worked" — production adds accountability, audit, and compliance the pilot never had; without review it's an incident waiting to happen
Treating "works in a demo" as a readiness criterion — without objective evals and quality thresholds, degradation is only noticed via user complaints
Rolling out to 100% at once with no rollback plan — the first failure hits everyone, with nowhere to fall back
Ignoring cost until the end-of-month invoice — token and API spend grows nonlinearly at scale
Leaving prompts "floating" without versioning — you can't tell which change broke quality in prod

exercises.question: Write 3-5 measurable readiness criteria for your pilot going to prod (not "it works", but with numbers). What do you measure and what threshold counts as passing?
exercises.hint: Think about share of correct answers on a reference set, p95 response time, error rate, and cost per request. Each criterion needs a concrete threshold number.

exercises.question: Describe the rollback plan for your release: on what signal do you roll back, how fast, and to where exactly (to the pilot, a manual process, the previous version)?
exercises.hint: Tie the rollback trigger to monitoring metrics (error spike, quality drop, cost surge) and make sure the previous state is preserved and reachable within minutes.

exercises.question: List the data types flowing through your AI system and classify them by sensitivity. Where do you need access restrictions or governance sign-off?
exercises.hint: Split data into public / internal / personal / confidential. For personal and confidential, check the DPA with the model vendor and who has access to logs.

s1.title: Pilot readiness criteria
s1.why: "The pilot works" is not a criterion. Without measurable thresholds you can't tell a finished system from a lucky demo, and the rollout decision rests on gut feel.
instructions: Audit the pilot: what exactly it does, on what data, and its boundaries (what it must NOT do)
Define 3-5 measurable readiness criteria with threshold numbers (accuracy, response time, error rate, cost per request)
Fix the scope of the first rollout: which share of users/processes goes to prod first
Describe the target workflow architecture and where prompts live — relates to the [[node:use-cases|use case]] scenario
s1.validate: There is a document with 3-5 readiness criteria, each with a concrete threshold and measurement method.
s1.tip: Derive criteria from the pilot's real risks, not from a template: what breaks first under more load or new data.

s2.title: Reliability and error handling
s2.why: A pilot forgives failures — production doesn't. Model timeouts, garbage output, and peak load must be handled predictably instead of failing onto the user.
instructions: List failure points: model timeout/unavailability, invalid or incomplete output, limit overruns
For each, define behavior: retry with backoff, fallback response, degrade to a manual process
Add validation of model output before it reaches the user or the next step
Freeze and version all prompts — every change must be traceable
Establish formal quality gates in the workflow
s2.validate: Every failure point has defined behavior, prompts are versioned, and model output is validated before use.
s2.tip: The most common production failure isn't "the model went down" but "the model returned plausible garbage." Format and sanity validation matter more than retries.

s3.title: Quality evaluation and evals
s3.why: Without objective evaluation, quality degradation is only noticed via complaints. Evals turn "we think it's better" into a reproducible number before rollout.
instructions: Build a reference set (golden set) with expected results — study the [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|approach to evals and benchmarks]]
Define quality metrics for your task (correctness, relevance, output safety)
Set a passing threshold: below it, no rollout proceeds
Run evals on every prompt or model change — it's part of the quality gate
s3.validate: There is a golden set and a metric set; an eval run produces a number comparable to the readiness threshold from step 1.
s3.tip: Start with 20-50 representative examples, including edge and "harmful" cases. A small honest set beats a large formal one.

s4.title: Monitoring and cost
s4.why: In prod you can't fly blind: quality drifts, load grows, and token/API spend scales nonlinearly. Without observability you're the last to see the problem.
instructions: Set up monitoring of key metrics: quality, error rate, response time, request volume
Enable cost tracking per request and per day, with a spike alert — see [[node:ai-operations|AI operations]] practices
Create a dashboard and threshold alerts tied to the readiness criteria from step 1
Log inputs/outputs (privacy-aware) for incident analysis and enriching evals
s4.validate: The dashboard shows quality, errors, latency, and cost in real time; alerts are configured for threshold breaches.
s4.tip: Wire the quality alert directly to the rollback trigger from step 6 — monitoring is useless if no one acts on it.

s5.title: Security and access
s5.why: Production adds accountability, audit, and compliance the pilot never had. The governance review takes 1-2 weeks but saves months and prevents incidents.
instructions: Classify the data flowing through the system (public / internal / personal / confidential)
Check the DPA with the model vendor and terms for processing sensitive data
Restrict access on a least-privilege basis: who sees logs, prompts, outputs
Identify AI-specific risks (data leakage, prompt injection, harmful output) and capture mitigations
Obtain governance approval before rollout
s5.validate: Data is classified, access is restricted, risks with mitigations are documented, and governance sign-off exists.
s5.tip: Don't treat governance as bureaucracy: one documented risk with a mitigation is cheaper than one incident review with a regulator.

s6.title: Rollout, rollback plan, and checklist
s6.why: Releasing to 100% at once with no rollback is all-in. A gradual rollout with a ready rollback turns a failure from a catastrophe into a manageable episode.
instructions: Roll out gradually (canary / by traffic share), watching the step-4 metrics at each stage
Describe the rollback plan: trigger signal, speed, target state (pilot / manual process / previous version)
Ensure the previous state is preserved and rollback takes minutes
Run the final readiness checklist: criteria (s1), reliability (s2), evals above threshold (s3), monitoring and alerts (s4), governance approval (s5)
After reaching 100%, observe for 90 days and iterate on monitoring data
s6.validate: The system reached full traffic via a gradual rollout; the rollback plan is tested; the 5-item checklist is closed.
s6.tip: Rehearse the rollback before the release. A rollback plan you've never run usually fails at the moment of an incident.

uc-ai-roi-estimation.title: Estimate AI Project ROI Before Launch
uc-ai-roi-estimation.subtitle: 6 steps from "AI will help" to "AI will deliver $X over Y months"
uc-ai-roi-estimation.whatItIs:
AI projects often fail to get budget because of "unclear ROI". This scenario turns the vague "AI will help" into a concrete "AI will deliver $X over Y months". You define value and metrics, count real costs (tokens, time, infrastructure), record a "before" baseline, build a benefit and payback model, document risks and assumptions — and make a go/no-go decision.

It builds on the structured approach from [[node:en-roi-measurement|ROI Measurement]]: baseline → projection → measurement → iteration. Part of the [[node:use-cases|use-case]] collection.
uc-ai-roi-estimation.approach: Don't count only direct cost savings. AI brings 5 value categories: time savings + quality improvement + new capabilities + risk reduction + future optionality. Without all five, ROI looks low and the project gets cancelled prematurely. Be honest about assumptions — separately mark what is proven and what is a guess.
outcomes: Value categories and measurable project metrics defined
All costs counted: tokens, working time, infrastructure
"Before AI" baseline recorded on historical data
Benefit and payback model built (best/expected/worst)
Justified go/no-go decision made with a checklist

applyIn.title: Before a budget request
applyIn.description: You come to leadership not with "AI will help" but with numbers, a range, and a payback period.

applyIn.title: Quarterly review of AI projects
applyIn.description: Compare real ROI against the projection — refine the model and decide whether to continue or wind down.

applyIn.title: Investment prioritization
applyIn.description: Compare an AI initiative against other investments in the same language — money and timelines.

pitfalls: Counting only direct cost savings — without quality, speed, and risk reduction, ROI is understated.
Forgetting token and infrastructure costs — expenses look smaller than reality and the projection breaks.
Not recording a "before" baseline — later there is no way to prove the benefit is real.
Presenting a single optimistic scenario — without a worst case, leadership won't trust the numbers.
Hiding assumptions inside the calculations — under scrutiny the model collapses and trust is lost.

exercises.question: Take a specific AI initiative and list its value across all 5 categories (time, quality, capabilities, risk, optionality). How many categories did you miss at first?
exercises.hint: If your list contains only "cost savings", you are underestimating the project at least twofold.

exercises.question: Calculate the monthly token cost for your scenario: average request size × number of requests × price. Compare it with the salaried time the project saves.
exercises.hint: Token cost is almost always lower than the working time saved — that is the core of the ROI.

exercises.question: Build a 5-point go/no-go checklist for your initiative. Which point can't be marked "yes" right now?
exercises.hint: The point you can't check is your main risk — close it before launch.

s1.title: Define value and metrics
s1.why: Without a clear answer to "what value does the project create and how is it measured", any ROI is fantasy. Value first, money second.
instructions: Describe the problem the AI initiative solves in a single sentence.
List value across 5 categories: time savings, quality, new capabilities, risk reduction, future optionality.
For each category pick 1-2 measurable metrics (e.g. hours per month, % errors, response speed).
Mark which metrics can be pulled from existing data and which you need to start measuring.
s1.validate: You have a list of value categories, each with a concrete metric you can actually measure.
s1.tip: If a metric has no data source, it's not a metric — it's a wish. Replace it with something you can count.

s2.title: Count costs: tokens, time, infrastructure
s2.why: ROI is benefit minus cost. Understated costs produce a pretty projection that falls apart in practice.
instructions: Estimate token cost: average request size × requests per month × model price. Lean on [[node:sys-cost-management|cost management]].
Add working time: development, integration, support, training people.
Account for infrastructure: hosting, storage, third-party services, monitoring.
Split costs into one-off (launch) and recurring (monthly).
s2.validate: You have a full cost total split into one-off and recurring, with no forgotten line items.
s2.tip: Add a 20-30% buffer on tokens: real consumption is almost always higher than the first estimate due to retries and context.

s3.title: Record the "before" baseline
s3.why: Without a "how it was before AI" reference point, you cannot prove the benefit is real rather than coincidence.
instructions: Gather historical data on the chosen metrics for 60-90 days (if possible).
Record current values: how much time, money, and errors it takes today without AI.
If there is no history, measure manually for at least 1-2 weeks before launch.
Save the baseline separately: it's the reference you'll compare the real result against.
s3.validate: You have recorded "before AI" numbers for each key metric.
s3.tip: Take dated screenshots and exports of the baseline. In a quarter, no one will remember how it was without recorded figures.

s4.title: Build the benefit and payback model
s4.why: Leadership needs not promises but a range and a timeline: when the project pays back and how much it brings.
instructions: Build three benefit scenarios: pessimistic, expected, optimistic.
For each, compute ROI = (benefit − cost) / cost and the payback period (when cumulative benefit covers the investment).
Use Claude to check the calculations and formulas — based on [[node:en-roi-measurement|ROI Measurement]].
Bring it all into one table: costs, benefit by category, ROI, payback period — across the three scenarios.
s4.validate: You have a table with three scenarios, an ROI figure, and a payback period in each.
s4.tip: Show the expected scenario as the main one, but always keep the worst case next to it. That earns more trust than a single optimistic projection.

s5.title: Document risks and assumptions
s5.why: Any ROI model stands on assumptions. If you don't surface them, the model collapses at the first review and trust evaporates.
instructions: Write out all model assumptions: expected usage volume, token price, adoption speed, people's behavior.
For each assumption, mark whether it's proven by data or a guess.
List risks: rising token cost, low adoption by people, model changes, technical failures.
For each risk, note the impact on ROI and a mitigation plan.
s5.validate: You have a list of assumptions marked "proven/guess" and a risk table with mitigation plans.
s5.tip: The most dangerous assumption is usage volume. If people don't adopt the tool, the benefit zeroes out while the costs remain.

s6.title: Make the go/no-go decision and build a checklist
s6.why: All this work serves one purpose: a justified decision to launch or not, and a clear measurement plan for afterward.
instructions: Build a 5-7 point go/no-go checklist: positive ROI in the expected scenario, acceptable payback period, key risks closed, baseline recorded, measurement system ready.
Run through the checklist: if even one critical point is "no", it's a no-go or needs rework.
Describe the measurement plan: which metrics, how often to reconcile real ROI against the projection.
Schedule a quarterly review: real vs projected, model refinement.
Record the decision and rationale in a single document for leadership.
s6.validate: You have a completed checklist, an explicit go/no-go decision, and a post-launch measurement plan.
s6.tip: A no-go decision is also a valuable result: you saved the budget by not spending it on a project with negative ROI.

uc-ai-vendor-selection.title: AI Vendor and Stack Selection
uc-ai-vendor-selection.subtitle: How to choose an LLM provider and stack by explicit criteria, not hype
uc-ai-vendor-selection.whatItIs: A structured course for choosing AI tools: LLM provider, vector DB, monitoring, integrations. Instead of asking "which Claude/GPT/Open Source?", you get a repeatable process with explicit criteria, a pilot on your own tasks, and a documented decision.
uc-ai-vendor-selection.approach: First fix requirements and weighted criteria. Then build a long list of options, narrow to 3-5, and score on capability, cost, privacy, and lock-in. Next run a blind pilot on 10 representative tasks, do a security/compliance check, and make the final decision with a rollout plan. Built on [[node:pl-compare|platform comparison]], [[node:pl-api|API economics]], and [[node:use-cases|use cases]].
outcomes: A documented vendor decision with reasoning in 2-3 weeks
A weighted criteria matrix tied to your task, not to marketing
Blind pilot results on 10 representative tasks
A security and compliance checklist (DPA, encryption, audit logs)
A rollout plan with a fallback strategy and lock-in risk assessment

applyIn.title: Before a major AI initiative
applyIn.description: An investment above $50k demands explicit criteria and a pilot, not a single-benchmark decision.

applyIn.title: Annual technology review
applyIn.description: Reassess the stack: is the current vendor still best on cost, quality, and stability.

applyIn.title: Replacing an unreliable vendor
applyIn.description: When the current provider degrades or lock-in risk rises, you need a structured reassessment and fallback.

pitfalls: Deciding on a single public benchmark — it is biased and measures generic capabilities, not your task
Ignoring lock-in: no data portability or API abstraction makes future migration impossible
Comparing only on price per token without weighing quality, latency, and support
Skipping the privacy and compliance check before signing the contract
Piloting on toy examples instead of 10 real representative tasks

exercises.question: Build a matrix of 7 criteria (quality, cost, latency, security, vendor stability, lock-in, support) and assign weights summing to 100%. Which criterion got the highest weight and why is it the one for your task?
exercises.hint: Weights should reflect real pain: if data is sensitive, security weighs more; if load is high, latency and cost matter most.

exercises.question: Collect 10 representative tasks from your real workflow and describe how you would run a blind test of 3-5 vendors to remove bias.
exercises.hint: Hide vendor names during scoring, fix success criteria in advance, and score everyone identically.

exercises.question: For your top 2 vendors, describe a fallback strategy: what happens if one shuts down or doubles its price?
exercises.hint: Think about data portability, API abstraction, and migration time in days/weeks.

s1.title: Define criteria and requirements
s1.why: Without explicit weighted criteria, the decision slides toward hype and personal preference. Criteria are the foundation of the whole process.
instructions: State the concrete use case and constraints (budget, load, data type)
List 7 criteria: quality, cost, latency, security, vendor stability, lock-in, support
Assign weights summing to 100% based on your actual pain
Separate threshold must-have requirements from nice-to-have ones
s1.validate: You have a table of 7 weighted criteria summing to 100% and a list of must-have requirements.
s1.tip: Set the weights BEFORE looking at options — otherwise you will tune them to fit a vendor you already like.

s2.title: Build a long list of options
s2.why: A broad list up front protects against tunnel vision: the best option may sit outside the "obvious three".
instructions: Gather 8-12 candidates: proprietary LLMs, open source, specialized providers
Study platform differences via [[node:pl-compare|platform comparison]]: web, Code, API, and others
Note for each: API availability, pricing model, data residency region
Filter by must-have requirements from step 1 down to a short list of 3-5
s2.validate: A long list of 8-12 options is narrowed to a justified short list of 3-5 candidates.
s2.tip: Do not drop open source too early — for private data it is often the optimal choice.

s3.title: Score capability, cost, privacy, and lock-in
s3.why: This is where criteria turn into numbers. Price per token without weighing quality and lock-in is a trap that surfaces in six months.
instructions: Compute economics via [[node:pl-api|API economics]]: price per million tokens, rate limits, projected monthly cost
Score each model's capability on your task type, not on generic benchmarks
Check privacy: where data is stored and whether your data is used for training
Assess lock-in: data portability and the ability to abstract the API
Fill the step 1 matrix with preliminary scores for each candidate
s3.validate: The criteria matrix is filled with numbers for all 3-5 candidates, including projected monthly cost.
s3.tip: Count total cost of ownership, not just price per token: integration, monitoring, and migration also cost money.

s4.title: Run a pilot on your own task
s4.why: This is the key real-world signal. Benchmarks are biased — only a blind test on your tasks shows the truth.
instructions: Take 10 representative tasks from your real workflow
Run them through each short-list candidate under identical conditions
Run blind scoring: hide vendor names when assigning scores
Record quality, latency (p50/p99), and run cost for each
Update the criteria matrix with real pilot data
s4.validate: You have blind scores for 3-5 vendors on 10 real tasks with measured quality, latency, and cost.
s4.tip: Fix success criteria before launching the pilot — otherwise scoring becomes subjective.

s5.title: Check security and compliance
s5.why: The technically best vendor is useless if it fails DPA, data residency, or audit requirements. This is a blocking filter.
instructions: Request the DPA and verify personal data processing terms
Check data residency region and alignment with your requirements
Confirm encryption and audit logs are available
For integrations, assess the access and connection model via [[node:mcp|MCP]]
Build a security review checklist and run it against each finalist
s5.validate: Each finalist passed the security checklist: DPA, data residency, encryption, audit logs are checked off.
s5.tip: Compliance is a go/no-go filter: a vendor failing a must-have on security drops out regardless of quality.

s6.title: Decide and build the rollout plan
s6.why: A documented decision with reasoning lets you assess in six months whether it was the right call and reduces vendor churn.
instructions: Aggregate the weighted scores from the matrix and pick the winner
Run final negotiations on price and SLA
Describe the fallback strategy: what to do on shutdown or a price hike
Build a rollout plan with phases and owners
Document the decision with reasoning and save it for the next review
s6.validate: A document is ready with the chosen vendor, reasoning, fallback strategy, and a rollout plan checklist.
s6.tip: Record a review date — in six months honestly assess whether it was the right choice.

uc-ai-multi-agent-system.title: Multi-Agent System: Orchestration
uc-ai-multi-agent-system.subtitle: How to build a system of several agents without drowning in complexity
uc-ai-multi-agent-system.whatItIs: This is the path to a working multi-agent system: several specialized agents, coordination between them, context passing, and error recovery. A scenario for technical teams that hit the limit of a single agent and want to split the task into roles. See the [[node:use-cases|use cases]] section and the [[node:agents|agents]] foundation.
uc-ai-multi-agent-system.approach: The principle is simple: multi-agent is not «more agents = better», but an answer to a concrete limit. First you prove a single agent is exhausted (prompts, tools, RAG no longer help), then you decompose the task into roles, design the handoff protocol and orchestrator, give each agent its tools and boundaries, add observability, and only then roll out. Complexity grows quadratically, so every step is a deliberate decision, not an automatic upgrade.
outcomes: You understand when multi-agent is justified and when one agent is enough
You can decompose a task into clear roles without overlapping responsibilities
You designed the handoff protocol and the orchestrator role
Each agent has explicit tools, boundaries, and clear input/output
Observability is set up: structured logs and the ability to replay a failure

applyIn.title: Complex research pipeline
applyIn.description: One agent gathers sources, another fact-checks, a third synthesizes the report — the orchestrator links the stages and catches failures.

applyIn.title: Development with review
applyIn.description: An agent writes code, a critic agent reviews, another runs tests — each with its own expertise and boundaries.

applyIn.title: Parallel task processing
applyIn.description: A task with independent subtasks of different expertise is parallelized across agents, and the orchestrator assembles the result.

pitfalls: Jumping into multi-agent from nothing: if a single agent feels limited, first improve prompts, tools, and RAG
Blurry roles: two agents own the same thing and it is unclear who makes the decision
No handoff protocol: agents exchange data «however», and context is lost between steps
No observability: a failure cannot be reproduced and debugging turns into guesswork
Ignoring rising cost and latency: every extra agent adds calls, money, and delay

exercises.question: Take a task currently handled by one agent. Prove in 3 points that it is truly exhausted — or admit multi-agent is not needed.
exercises.hint: Check in turn: prompt improvement, adding tools, RAG. If any one of them yields a gain, the limit is not reached yet.

exercises.question: Decompose your task into 2-3 roles and describe for each: input, output, tools, boundaries.
exercises.hint: Roles must not overlap. If two roles fight over one decision, you need an orchestrator — or it is a single role.

exercises.question: Describe the handoff protocol between two agents: what exactly is passed, in what format, what to do on error.
exercises.hint: Rely on patterns from [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff protocols]] — a structured format beats free text.

s1.title: Decide: do you even need multi-agent
s1.why: Multi-agent adds complexity quadratically — debugging, monitoring, cost, latency. Launching it without a proven single-agent limit means paying a high price for nothing.
instructions: State the current task and where the single agent «hits the wall»
Check the three single-agent levers: better prompts, more tools, RAG
Record whether the task has clear subtasks with different expertise or needs parallelism
Make the decision explicit: move to multi-agent or stay on one agent
s1.validate: You have a written justification of 3+ points why one agent is not enough — or a decision to stay on one.
s1.tip: Heuristic: multi-agent is usually justified after 6+ months of single-agent experience. If you are unsure, you are not at the limit yet.

s2.title: Decompose into roles and agents
s2.why: The strength of multi-agent is specialization. Clear, non-overlapping roles turn one large task into a set of manageable, testable units.
instructions: Break the task into subtasks and group them by expertise
Assign each group an agent role with a single area of responsibility
Choose an architectural pattern: coordinator-worker, debate, reflection, or tool-using agent
Verify roles do not overlap and that each has a clear input and output
s2.validate: You have a list of 2-3 roles, each with one area of responsibility and no overlap; an architectural pattern is chosen.
s2.tip: Rely on [[node:sys-multi-agent-patterns|multi-agent system patterns]]: coordinator-worker is the most common and predictable starting point.

s3.title: Handoff protocol and orchestrator
s3.why: Context is lost between agents if the exchange is «however it goes». An explicit handoff protocol and an orchestrator role keep the system from chaos as the number of steps grows.
instructions: Define the orchestrator: who delegates, collects results, and makes the final decision
Describe the handoff format between agents — what exactly is passed and in what structure
Set recovery rules: what to do if an agent returns an error or garbage
Describe how context flows along the chain so nothing critical is lost
s3.validate: For every handoff between agents, the format is fixed and the on-error behavior is described.
s3.tip: A structured handoff format (see [[node:sys-handoff-protocols|handoff protocols]]) is more reliable than free text — it is easier to validate and replay.

s4.title: Tools and boundaries of each agent
s4.why: An agent without clear boundaries starts doing someone else's job or oversteps. An explicit set of tools and limits makes behavior predictable and safe.
instructions: For each agent, list the tools it actually needs
Set boundaries: what the agent does NOT do and where it hands work onward
Build and test each agent in isolation, before composition
If you work in Claude Code, implement roles via [[node:cc-subagents|subagents]]
s4.validate: Each agent is built and verified alone: on typical inputs it gives the expected output without overstepping its boundaries.
s4.tip: Minimize tools per agent: an extra tool is an extra way to fail and an extra call cost.

s5.title: Verification and observability
s5.why: Failures in multi-agent arise at the seams — in coordination, not inside a single agent. Without logs and replay, debugging turns into guesswork.
instructions: Add structured logging on every step: input, output, which agent, which decision
Ensure you can replay a failed run from the logs
Compose the agents into the full scenario and run end-to-end tests
Iterate specifically on coordination failures, not on individual agent quality
s5.validate: Any failure can be replayed from the logs and pinned to the agent seam where it occurred.
s5.tip: Compare metrics against the single-agent baseline: completion rate, latency, cost per completed scenario — otherwise you can't see whether the complexity paid off.

s6.title: Rollout and checklist
s6.why: The system is ready for production only when roles, protocol, boundaries, and observability are closed together. The checklist prevents shipping a half-assembled system.
instructions: Run the checklist: single-agent limit proven, roles non-overlapping, protocol described, boundaries set, logs and replay working
Fix baseline metrics and the thresholds at which the system is rolled back
Roll out on limited traffic and watch the agent seams
Build in an iteration loop: catch coordination failures and tune the protocol
s6.validate: All checklist items are closed, metrics are collected, and there is a clear rollback path on degradation.
s6.tip: Don't expand the number of agents «just in case». Add a role only when a concrete subtask proves it needs separate expertise.

uc-ai-design-research-launch.title: Launch AI Design Research
uc-ai-design-research-launch.subtitle: From a mountain of unread research material to a working AI synthesis pipeline in 6 steps
uc-ai-design-research-launch.whatItIs: A step-by-step scenario for turning accumulated interviews, session recordings, and user feedback into structured insights with AI — and embedding it into the team's ongoing design process. It is part of the [[node:use-cases|cross-layer scenarios]] collection and grounds the idea of [[node:ai-native-design|AI-native design]] in a concrete research cycle.
uc-ai-design-research-launch.approach: We move from data to decisions: first confirm the scenario is even warranted, then gather material into one place, run AI synthesis, rigorously check the findings for hallucination, turn patterns into design decisions, and lock it in as a repeatable process. AI accelerates synthesis, but a human remains accountable for the final insight.
outcomes: Know when AI Design Research delivers real value and when it is premature
Can consolidate scattered research material into a single AI-ready base
Get a repeatable synthesis prompt cycle: from transcripts to patterns in hours, not weeks
Tell a confirmed insight from a model hallucination and know how to verify it
Embed the research pipeline into the design process so the whole team uses it

applyIn.title: Accumulated research backlog
applyIn.description: The team has ≥10 session recordings or interview transcripts that no one has time to process — the scenario clears this backlog.

applyIn.title: Unbalanced design ops
applyIn.description: Lots of research input, little synthesis output: designers drown in data instead of designing. The pipeline restores the balance.

applyIn.title: Regular discovery cycles
applyIn.description: The team runs research every sprint and wants synthesis to stop being the bottleneck on every round.

pitfalls: Launching without PM alignment: design research and product research live separately, and a designers-only pipeline leads to duplicated work by PMs
Blindly trusting AI synthesis: the model elegantly states a pattern that is not in the data — without citation checks the insight is a hallucination
Starting without Head of Design buy-in: without leadership support the pipeline does not take root and stays a personal experiment
Trying to process the whole archive at once: better to tune synthesis on 5 sessions than get garbage on 50
Insights stay in a separate document and never reach design decisions — research for research's sake

exercises.question: Your team has 8 interview transcripts and no agreement with PMs. Should you launch the full AI Design Research pipeline right now?
exercises.hint: Check the entry conditions: the ≥10 materials threshold and mandatory PM alignment. What is missing and what should you fix before launch?

exercises.question: AI surfaced a pattern "users want dark mode", but only one person mentioned it in the sources. How do you catch this?
exercises.hint: Think about the verification step: every pattern must rest on citations from multiple sources, otherwise it is noise.

exercises.question: Synthesis is done, insights are structured — but the team's design does not change. Which step of the scenario was skipped or done only formally?
exercises.hint: Recall the difference between "turn insights into decisions" and "embed into the process". Where does the chain from data to product break?

s1.title: Understand when the scenario is needed and fix the outcome
s1.why: Launching the pipeline without the conditions met is the most expensive mistake: the team spends two weeks only to find there is nothing to synthesize or no one to use it.
instructions: Check the entry threshold: are there ≥10 session recordings or interview transcripts to process
Assess the design ops balance: lots of research input, little synthesis output is the signal to launch
Get buy-in from the Head of Design and agree on alignment with the PM team upfront
Fix the target outcome in measurable terms: time-to-insight, research coverage, a theme library
s1.validate: You hold three "yeses": enough material, leadership support, agreement with PMs — and the target metrics are written down.
s1.tip: If even one condition is unmet, do not launch the full pipeline — close the gap first. That is cheaper than rolling back a failed launch.

s2.title: Consolidate research material into a single base
s2.why: AI cannot synthesize what is scattered across drives, chats, and notes. A single indexed base is the foundation without which synthesis is impossible.
instructions: Gather all session recordings, interview transcripts, and user feedback into one place
Normalize the material to a single format: text with a source and date for each fragment
Create a dedicated "Design Research" workspace and load the full corpus into it
Index the material so it can be searched and specific fragments can be referenced
s2.validate: Any piece of research material is found on request within seconds, and the source is known for every fragment.
s2.tip: Keep the link from fragment to source from the start — you will need it at the verification step to prove an insight was not made up.

s3.title: Synthesize patterns with AI
s3.why: This is the core of the scenario: here hours of manual review turn into minutes, and a mountain of data into a set of recurring themes.
instructions: Formulate the synthesis prompt: ask to extract recurring themes, pains, and needs with their frequency
Run synthesis on 5 sessions first, not the whole archive — to tune the wording cheaply
Require the model to provide supporting citations for every extracted pattern
Group the result into a structured theme library, building on the [[node:ds-design-research|design research synthesis]] workflow
s3.validate: On the trial 5 sessions you have a draft list of patterns, each tied to specific fragments of the material.
s3.tip: A single prompt is rarely perfect on the first try: expect 2-3 iterations before the wording reliably yields useful output.

s4.title: Verify the findings — is it made up
s4.why: The model can convincingly state a pattern that is not in the data. Without an explicit check the team will decide based on a hallucination.
instructions: For each pattern open the supporting citations and compare them to the source fragment
Discard patterns resting on a single mention — that is noise, not a trend
Have a designer manually validate the draft synthesis on the same 5 sessions
Flag themes where AI overstated frequency or assigned meaning that was not there
s4.validate: Only patterns confirmed by several independent sources remain in the theme library; doubtful ones are flagged or removed.
s4.tip: Adopt a simple rule: a pattern without at least two sources is not an insight, it stays a hypothesis.

s5.title: Turn insights into design decisions
s5.why: A verified pattern is not yet a result. Value appears only when an insight turns into a concrete action for the product.
instructions: For each confirmed pattern, state which design decision it dictates
Link the insight to the specific screen, flow, or feature it changes
Prioritize: what changes now, what goes to backlog, what needs further checking
Capture the "insight → decision" statement so a designer outside the research context understands it
s5.validate: Each key insight is turned into a concrete, prioritized design action tied to the product.
s5.tip: Phrase the decision as "because [insight], we do [action]" — this keeps insights from settling as dead weight in a document.

s6.title: Embed into the design process and lock in with a checklist
s6.why: A one-off synthesis does not change a team. Value comes from a repeatable pipeline built into every research round and used by everyone.
instructions: Run team training and the first real research round on the new pipeline together
Sync the process with the PM team so design and product research yield shared insights instead of duplicating each other
Lock in the round checklist: material gathered → synthesis run → findings verified → insights turned into decisions
Assign an owner for maintaining the theme base and the cadence of rounds
s6.validate: The team runs the full cycle by the checklist on its own, insights reach decisions, and the PM team is connected to the shared theme library.
s6.tip: If you later want to automate collection and the first pass — look toward the [[node:agent-researcher|researcher agent]], which removes the routine of the first round.

uc-ai-personalization-launch.title: Launch AI Personalization in the Store
uc-ai-personalization-launch.subtitle: From generic UX for everyone to working personalization for returning customers — in 6 steps, no ML team required
uc-ai-personalization-launch.whatItIs: A practical path to launching AI personalization in e-commerce: you turn a one-size-fits-all storefront into personal recommendations for returning customers. It builds on [[node:ai-native-ecommerce|AI-native e-commerce]] and embeddings ([[node:af-embeddings|af-embeddings]]) — without a data science team and without heavy ML infrastructure. Real scope: 6-8 weeks, 1-2 people.
uc-ai-personalization-launch.approach: First validate that personalization is even needed and where it delivers impact, then prepare user data with respect for privacy, build segments and recommendation logic, embed it into the storefront, measure the effect via A/B, and only then scale. The principle: start where returning traffic is highest (home page), not where it "seems cheaper" (email).
outcomes: Understand when personalization is justified (catalog >1k SKUs, >5k active returning customers) and what result is realistic
Collect user behavior data legally and transparently, with explicit consent and a fallback for new customers
Build segments and recommendation logic on embeddings without training your own ML models
Embed personalization into real storefront surfaces (home page, product page) with cold-start protection
Prove uplift via A/B vs control: returning conversion +30-50%, AOV +10-25%, retention +15-30%

applyIn.title: Store home page
applyIn.description: A personal selection for the returning customer instead of the same banner — the main impact point, because most loyal traffic lands there.

applyIn.title: Product page and catalog
applyIn.description: A "similar / fits you" block based on product embeddings and view history instead of manual "frequently bought with" rules.

applyIn.title: Email and retention campaigns
applyIn.description: Personal triggered emails as a second wave — after the home page proves uplift, reuse the same recommendation logic.

pitfalls: Starting with email personalization: looks cheaper, but returning users more often come directly to the site — start with home page recommendations
No cold-start handling: a new user has no data, so the fallback must be generic but not "we don't know you"
Launching without measurement: without A/B vs control you can't prove AI personalization beats generic UX or tell uplift from seasonality
Collecting data without consent and transparency: personalization on "dark" data creates legal and reputational risk
Assuming you need an ML team: embeddings and retrieval cover 80% of cases without training your own models — don't delay over an imaginary entry barrier

exercises.question: You have 800 SKUs and 2k returning customers per month. Should you launch AI personalization right now?
exercises.hint: Check the entry thresholds: catalog >1k SKUs and >5k active returning customers. Consider whether there's enough data for segments to be meaningful rather than noise.

exercises.question: The team wants to build personal emails first because "the integration is simpler." What do you say?
exercises.hint: Where does most returning traffic live and where will you see impact faster? Recall the classic email vs home page mistake.

exercises.question: After the A/B test the persona group showed +12% conversion, but control also grew +9%. What is the real uplift and what does it mean?
exercises.hint: Uplift is the difference between the variant and control, not the absolute increase. Think about seasonality and why a control group is essential.

s1.title: Decide whether you need personalization and what result you'll get
s1.why: Personalization is the highest-ROI e-commerce case, but it isn't always justified. Without checking entry thresholds you'll spend 6-8 weeks on infrastructure that lacks the data to work.
instructions: Check the thresholds: catalog >1k SKUs and >5k active returning customers — otherwise there's too little data for meaningful segments
State the business goal in numbers: returning conversion +30-50%, AOV +10-25%, or retention +15-30%
Pick one starting surface with the highest returning traffic — usually the home page, not email
Assemble a minimal team: senior engineer + product manager + analyst, and confirm readiness for 6-8 weeks
Study the AI-native context in [[node:ai-native-ecommerce|AI-native e-commerce]] so you don't build ML infra where embeddings suffice
s1.validate: You have a written goal in metrics, a chosen starting surface, and a confirmed team for 6-8 weeks.
s1.tip: If the returning-customer threshold isn't met, don't launch — grow your loyal audience first. Personalization on noise is worse than honest generic UX.

s2.title: Collect user data — legally and transparently
s2.why: Personalization only works on behavior data. But data collected without consent is a legal and reputational risk that cancels out any uplift.
instructions: Define a minimal signal set: views, add-to-cart, purchases, session history — without over-collecting
Set up explicit user consent and a clear policy: what you collect and why
Tie data to a stable returning-customer identifier and ensure it persists across sessions
Build a fallback for a new user with no history: a generic selection, but without phrasing it as "we don't know you"
Turn products into embeddings via [[node:af-embeddings|af-embeddings]] — the basis for comparison and recommendations without ML training
s2.validate: User signals are collected with consent, persisted across sessions, and products are represented as vectors; a working generic fallback exists for new customers.
s2.tip: Collect less but better: three strong signals (view, cart, purchase) deliver more than a dozen noisy ones.

s3.title: Build segments and recommendation logic
s3.why: Raw data doesn't personalize by itself — you need logic that links user behavior to fitting products. On embeddings this works without training your own models.
instructions: Define 3-5 behavioral segments (e.g., new, one-time, loyal, dormant) — don't fragment too finely
Describe the recommendation logic: embedding proximity of products to user history plus simple business rules (in stock, margin)
Study the retrieval pattern in [[node:sys-rag-architecture|sys-rag-architecture]] — the same one underpins finding similar products
Describe the concrete personalization workflow per [[node:ec-personalization|ec-personalization]] and the recommendation engine per [[node:ec-recommendations|ec-recommendations]]
Define fallback rules in advance: what to show on empty history and when no relevant matches exist
s3.validate: For any segment and user the system deterministically returns an ordered list of recommendations, and on empty history a correct generic fallback.
s3.tip: Don't chase dozens of segments. Four clear segments with sharp logic work better than twenty fuzzy ones.

s4.title: Embed personalization into the storefront
s4.why: Recommendation logic delivers value only when the user sees it. Integration into a real storefront surface is where the idea becomes a product.
instructions: Embed a personal block into the surface chosen in step 1 — start with the home page
Ensure a fast response: recommendations must render without a noticeable page delay
Wire the generic fallback into the UI so a new user sees a meaningful storefront, not emptiness
Instrument impressions and clicks on the personal block right away — without this there's nothing to measure in step 5
Verify edge cases: no history, item out of stock, recommendations empty
s4.validate: The personal block is visible in the real storefront, works correctly for returning and new users, and its impressions and clicks are tracked.
s4.tip: Don't roll out to 100% of traffic at once — keep a control group on generic UX; you'll need it at the measurement step.

s5.title: Measure the effect via A/B and metrics
s5.why: Without A/B vs control you can't tell real personalization uplift from seasonal growth, nor prove to the business that the investment paid off.
instructions: Run an A/B: persona group versus control on generic UX with the same audience
Compute uplift as the difference between groups, not the absolute increase — control filters out seasonality
Track key metrics: returning conversion, AOV, retention, plus the personal block's CTR
Let the test reach statistical significance; don't stop it after the first days
Record the result and decision: expand, refine the logic, or roll back
s5.validate: You have an A/B result with clear uplift relative to control and a decision based on it, backed by significant data rather than first impressions.
s5.tip: If control grew almost as much as the persona group, there's no real uplift — look for the cause in your recommendation logic instead of celebrating absolute growth.

s6.title: Scale and run the readiness checklist
s6.why: Proven uplift on one surface is the basis for expansion. Scaling without checking the foundation replicates mistakes onto new storefront surfaces.
instructions: Expand personalization to the next surfaces: product page, catalog, then email campaigns
Reuse the same recommendation logic and embeddings — don't build a new system per surface
Run the checklist: data consent in place, cold-start fallback works, A/B set up, metrics rising
Establish an iteration loop: refine segments and rules using data from new surfaces
Benchmark against [[node:use-cases|use-cases]] to keep the chain "goal → data → logic → measurement" intact
s6.validate: Personalization runs on at least two surfaces with proven uplift, the readiness checklist passes, and iterations are driven by data, not intuition.
s6.tip: Scale only what has already proven uplift. Porting unproven logic to new surfaces multiplies risk, not results.

uc-ai-product-search.title: Launch Semantic Catalog Search
uc-ai-product-search.subtitle: From "no results" to hybrid semantic search with reranking — in 6 steps
uc-ai-product-search.whatItIs: A scenario for launching semantic search on top of an existing keyword search in an e-commerce catalog. You don't throw away the old search — you add a vector layer built on [[node:af-embeddings|embeddings]] that understands the meaning of a query, not just exact words. The result is hybrid search: keyword handles exact SKU matches, semantic handles meaning and synonyms.
uc-ai-product-search.approach: Move from problem to production: first confirm that you genuinely need semantics (rather than a keyword fix), then prepare the catalog data, build embeddings and an index, add ranking and filters, measure quality on real queries, and only then roll out to the storefront under an A/B test. Every step produces a verifiable result so you don't build blind.
outcomes: You understand when semantics are truly needed versus just cleaning up keyword search
The catalog is prepared and turned into vectors, the index is built and re-indexes itself
Hybrid ranking works: keyword + semantic + availability and category filters
Search quality is measured with numbers (no-results rate, conversion, top clicks), not by feel
Search is rolled out to the storefront via an A/B test with a rollback path

applyIn.title: Large e-commerce catalog
applyIn.description: Catalog >5k SKUs where >15% of search sessions end in "no results" due to synonyms and phrasing.

applyIn.title: Multilingual storefront
applyIn.description: A site in several languages where keyword search fails to bridge queries and product descriptions across languages.

applyIn.title: Catalog with rich descriptions
applyIn.description: Products with detailed attributes and use cases that people search for "by meaning" rather than by exact name.

pitfalls: Replacing keyword search entirely: keyword wins on SKUs and exact codes — hybrid is mandatory
Not re-indexing the catalog: products change and sell out, and without index updates search shows out-of-stock items
Launching with no feedback loop: without click and purchase data, ranking never improves
Ignoring query analytics: AI searches well but doesn't explain why people search for "X" — that's a separate task
Rolling out with no A/B test: you can't prove the conversion lift and can't justify the embeddings cost

exercises.question: How do you use data to decide whether you need semantics or your keyword search quality is the problem?
exercises.hint: Look at the share of "no results" sessions and their queries: synonyms and phrasing mean you need semantics; typos and missing facets mean fix keyword.

exercises.question: Why is hybrid (keyword + semantic) better than pure semantics for a catalog?
exercises.hint: Semantics blurs exact matches on SKUs, codes and brands where keyword is more precise. Hybrid takes the best of both.

exercises.question: Which 3 metrics will you watch in the A/B test to call the launch a success?
exercises.hint: No-results rate, search conversion and time-to-first-click — all three should move the right way without a rise in complaints.

s1.title: Understand when semantics are needed and the target outcome
s1.why: Semantic search costs money on embeddings and infrastructure. Before building, you must prove the problem is genuinely about query meaning and not a broken keyword search. Otherwise you're solving the wrong problem.
instructions: Export search queries for 1-3 months and compute the share of sessions with "no results"
Label the failed queries: typos, missing facets are keyword; synonyms, meaning-based descriptions, other languages are semantic
Compare the scenario against neighboring cases in [[node:use-cases|use-cases]] so you don't rebuild a ready pattern
Fix the target outcome in numbers: no-results rate, search conversion, time-to-first-click
Decide the boundary: what stays with keyword (SKUs, codes) and what goes to semantics
s1.validate: You have a table of failed queries tagged "keyword/semantic" and the share of semantic failures is above the threshold that justifies the project.
s1.tip: If almost all failures are typos and missing filters, fix keyword first: it's cheaper and faster than semantics.

s2.title: Prepare the catalog and data
